author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Feminist Spaces: Abusive Power and the Accountability We Owe
content:
Feminist spaces are not toxic. Feminism is not toxic. Accountability is not toxic.


So, what is?


This began as my rage, but now it is my love letter to the movement.


A call to do better. To be better. To build spaces worthy of the feminism we claim.


This piece is born from my rage. From the nights I spent questioning whether I was too sensitive, too difficult, too much. From the moments I swallowed my truth because speaking it would cost me opportunities, contracts, references, relationships, or my place in the movement. From the realization that I was being asked to trade my voice for access, my dignity for opportunity, my growth for loyalty and the truth is… I am done trading.


I know I am not alone. This is not just my story. It is the story of countless women, feminists, workers, and young people who have been asked to choose between their voice and their livelihood, between their dignity and their place in the room.


Maybe you know this feeling. The tightness in your chest before a meeting. The way you edit yourself mid-sentence. The calculations you make:

If I say this, will I lose that contract? That reference? That place at the table?


What is toxic is expecting people to be silent because they were “given an opportunity,” as though a job, contract, platform, or salary bought permanent ownership of their voice. What is toxic is calling people ungrateful, difficult, arrogant, or “not humble” because they refuse to shrink themselves to make others comfortable. Humility is not silence. Gratitude is not obedience. Respect is not submission.


Maybe you have been told to fly but only within certain limits. Only as high as someone else is comfortable with. Only as far as someone else can control.


What is toxic is encouraging people to fly, but only if they do not fly too high, too far, too visibly, or beyond control. It is celebrating potential when it serves an image, then resenting growth when it reminds those in power that no one was ever theirs to own. You may have opened a door, but they walked through it. You may have offered an opportunity, but they brought the labour, talent, courage, ideas, and commitment.


None of us are self-made. We are made by community, by people who loved us, taught us, challenged us, believed in us, opened doors, and held us when we needed it.


But we also showed up. We did the work. We learned, took risks, survived uncertainty, and chose growth even when it meant leaving spaces that wanted us to doubt ourselves. You may have witnessed part of our journey, but you do not get to rewrite our story as though you made us.


Let us speak plainly about the people who “hold the keys to the city”. The keys to opportunities, the keys to funding, the keys to visibility, to platforms, to convenings, to donor rooms, to decision-making tables, the keys to who gets hired, who gets promoted, who gets credited, who gets erased. Holding the keys is not itself the problem. The problem is when those keys are used to gatekeep, to exclude, to concentrate power, and to decide who belongs and who is erased. That misuse of power, wielding exclusionary authority as if it were neutral administration—is anti-feminist. 


Paying homage is deeply feminist, and I will acknowledge people who have labored for the movement for years. They have given decades of their lives, their energy, their health, their relationships, their peace. They have stood on frontlines, organized communities, written proposals, managed crises, mentored young feminists, and carried burdens no one else could see.


ON YOUR SHOULDERS WE STAND. WE ARE GRATEFUL. WE HONOR YOU.


But gratitude does not mean silence. Honor does not mean immunity and laboring for the movement does not place anyone above reproach.


Feminism was born out of questioning. It was born of women and gender-diverse people looking at what the world called “normal” and saying: this is not right. This is not just. This must change.


Feminism questioned marriage laws that treated women as property. It questioned workplace policies that excluded women. It questioned medical systems that silenced women’s pain. It questioned political structures that erased women’s voices. It questioned religious doctrines that justified women’s subordination. It questioned cultural practices that normalized violence against women.


Women at community gathering in Ghana. Photo by Random Institute on Unsplash


Feminism itself is a practice of critical interrogation. It is a …

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: AFN draft for upcoming meeting with prime minister, premiers, calls for a First Nations-controlled wealth fund
content:
A draft position paper prepared by the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) for the upcoming First Nations-First Ministers Meeting (FNFMM) asks Prime Minister Mark Carney and Canada’s premiers to jointly develop a new First Nations-controlled sovereign wealth fund, financed in part by ongoing contributions from projects of national interest.


The paper, entitled Building Prosperity for All, and obtained by APTN News, says the fund should reach every First Nation, whether or not a project is near them and whether or not they consent to a project that proceeds. No nation’s settlement money or own-source revenue would be used. No nation would be required to join.


At the moment, Canada has established the Canada Strong Fund, an arm’s-length Crown corporation seeded with $25 billion and open to retail investors, focused on energy, critical minerals, infrastructure and advanced manufacturing, the paper says.


The fund has no First Nations component in its design so the AFN is proposing two options. Add a dedicated First Nations piece inside the existing fund, or create a separate institution that First Nations control.


How money will flow into the fund would be set by a National Benefits Sharing Framework, which First Ministers are also being asked to develop. The money would be reinvested and left in the fund rather than being paid out right away.


Each year, a set share of the investment returns – not the original money put in – would go to First Nations infrastructure priorities.


“Canada cannot build projects without First Nations territories,” the paper says. “The question this paper aims to answer is how all First Nations come to benefit from that development, through a National Benefit Sharing Framework and Sovereign Wealth Fund.”


Current arrangements do not do that, the draft argues. Impact-benefit agreements, loan guarantees and revenue-sharing deals all follow the geography and location of the project, leaving out other Indigenous communities across Canada who do not live near the project.


“Canada’s major projects agenda distributes benefits and impacts unevenly by design. Proximate First Nations can negotiate impact benefit agreements, while distant First Nations have no comparable route to the benefits Canada asserts are national.”


A national sovereign wealth fund, unconnected to any agreement, would carry no such implication, the paper says. Receiving a benefit “would not cure an infringement, settle a disagreement or relieve the Crown of its duties.”


Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at a press conference in Ottawa. Photo by: APTN


The paper ties the fund to closing the First Nations infrastructure gap, which it calls the largest unbuilt project in the country. Work done with Indigenous Services Canada put the cost of closing the gap by 2030 at $349.2 billion. The figure now stands at $376.1 billion. If action slips to 2040, the paper says, it reaches an estimated $527 billion.


According to the brief, National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has framed closing the gap as a major project inside Canada’s infrastructure agenda.


First Nations are already building community and regional sovereign wealth funds, the paper notes. Fisher River Cree Nation’s trust is designed so that only income is distributed and capital is protected, is cited as a model.


The Ontario First Nations Sovereign Wealth Fund and the North Shore Mi’kmaq Tribal Council’s Nikutik LP are others. The national proposal is meant to sit alongside that ecosystem, not replace it. Nations could hold their own fund, join a regional one, or do neither, and could change their minds.


APTN reached out to the AFN about the paper but did not hear back.


The meeting with the prime minister and Canada’s premiers is

scheduled for Oct. 26.

 No details have been shared from the Prime Minister’s Office yet.


When Carney met with First Nations in 2025, the meeting was closed to media and only the prime minister’s speech was public.


Read More:


First Nations along Pacific Link route denounce lack of consultation


Carney designates Pacific Link pipeline in the ‘national interest’


According to the brief, First Nations have four “specific asks” of the prime minister and premiers, including the sovereign wealth fund.


“Jointly develop a First Nations National Benefits Sharing Framework that protects consent, preserves Nation specific benefits and ownership to First Nations,” plus “Recognize closing the First Nations infrastructure gap as …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: New Lawsuit Seeks to Oust Kushner From Envoy Position Amid Profit-Seeking
content:
The lawsuit comes as Trump’s son-in-law faces scrutiny over conflicts of interest related to his diplomatic efforts.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A government watchdog has filed a lawsuit seeking to prohibit Jared Kushner from serving as special envoy for the Trump administration amid reports of conflicts of interest related to his role as a top Middle East negotiator.

The complaint, filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) on Wednesday, argues that courts should block Kushner from his role because he has not been subject to Senate approval and financial disclosure requirements that are required for people with his level of power.

CREW argues that such requirements, set out by the Constitution’s Appointments Clause and the Ethics in Government act of 1978, were instituted to ensure that government officials who wield such power as Kushner are properly vetted by lawmakers and the public. Kushner holds his position “in clear violation of these protections,” the lawsuit states.

“Jared Kushner is required to follow the Constitution and federal law, and if he has nothing to hide, he should welcome the opportunity to go through the Senate confirmation process and show the public everything is above board,” said CREW president Donald K. Sherman in a statement. “Instead, he has decided to act as though he is above the law and ignore it.”

The lawsuit comes after recent reports revealed overlapping interests between his private equity firm and the Middle Eastern parties that he negotiates with as a White House representative.

Earlier this month, CNN found that Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, holds the largest stake in a Tel Aviv-based company that has significant stakes in arms makers that supply the Israeli military.

Additionally, The New York Times reported that Kushner has been trying to raise $5 billion or more for Affinity from Middle Eastern states this year while he was representing the U.S. in negotiations in the region. This spring, Affinity reported $6 billion in assets, with 99 percent belonging to foreign investors such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates.

As President Donald Trump’s “special envoy for peace,” Kushner has led or been involved with numerous high-level diplomatic missions to the Middle East, including talks with Iran prior to the launch of the 2026 U.S.-Israeli war on the country, alongside fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff.

“The interplay and overlap between his government role and private business interests present a heightened risk of financial conflicts of interest,” CREW’s lawsuit states. “Nonetheless, Kushner continues to exercise significant government power while circumventing the very protections put in place to guard against such conflicts.”

The lawsuit also requests that the court requires Kushner to file financial disclosures covering his time as special envoy for peace.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Man dies after altercation in Iqaluit
content:
RCMP are treating the death of a man involved in an altercation in Iqaluit last week as a homicide.


Police responded to calls about an altercation at around 9:55 p.m. on Oct. 6, according to a press release issued Wednesday by Sgt. George Henrie.


Two people were transported to the Qikiqtani General Hospital with life-threatening injuries.


“Despite life saving measures, one male succumbed to his injuries,” Henrie wrote.


RCMP identified the man who died as 38-year-old Robert Kipanik.


The other person, who has yet to be identified, was medivaced to Ottawa, where he is in stable condition.


The RCMP’s Major Crime Unit is investigating.

author: David S. D'Amato
title: Jalan Libertarian Menuju Egalitarianisme
content:
Oleh:

David S. D’Amato

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

”. Diterjemahkan ke Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Sebuah studi terbaru dari

National Bureau of Economic Research

 yang dilakukan Emmanuel Saez dan Gabriel Zucman

 menemukan bahwa “

0,1% keluarga [di Amerika Serikat] yang berada di puncak distribusi kekayaan kini memiliki bagian kekayaan yang kira-kira sama dengan 90% keluarga yang berada di bagian terbawah.

” Lebih jauh, studi tersebut menunjukkan bahwa “pemulihan” ekonomi yang terus kita dengar ternyata belum sampai kepada kelas menengah. Hanya mereka yang berada di puncak piramida ekonomi yang benar-benar menikmati manfaatnya.


Ketika sebagian kecil penduduk menimbun begitu banyak kekayaan negara, para pakar kebijakan dan akademisi sibuk mencari pihak yang harus disalahkan sekaligus menawarkan berbagai solusi. Seperti yang bisa diduga, pasar bebas kemudian menjadi sasaran kritik sebagai sumber semakin lebarnya ketimpangan kekayaan dan pendapatan. Sebagai pendukung deregulasi dan pasar bebas, kaum libertarian sering dituduh hidup dalam dunia fantasi dan menutup mata terhadap persoalan ketimpangan.


Kami, kaum libertarian, sebenarnya ikut memperburuk keadaan. Ketika persoalan ini tak terhindarkan muncul, terlalu banyak dari kami justru terlihat gelisah dan bersikap defensif dengan bersikeras bahwa ketimpangan

sama sekali bukan

 masalah, bahwa yang seharusnya kita lihat adalah standar hidup atau ukuran lainnya. “Kapitalisme sangat baik bagi orang miskin—sumpah!” Kaum libertarian harus menerima kenyataan yang pahit bahwa ketimpangan memang merupakan persoalan yang sangat besar.


Namun, kita tidak perlu memandang ketimpangan sebagai titik lemah dalam argumen kita mengenai kebebasan ekonomi, atau sebagai persoalan yang tidak mungkin kita menangkan. Hubungan ekonomi yang ada saat ini bukanlah hasil dari kebebasan pertukaran maupun kepemilikan pribadi yang sah. Justru kaum libertarian berada pada posisi yang kuat dalam persoalan ketimpangan. Kebebasan dan kesetaraan pada kenyataannya saling melengkapi dan memperkuat satu sama lain; yang pertama secara alamiah menghasilkan yang kedua.


Kaum anarkis individualis seperti Lysander Spooner berpendapat bahwa “ekstrem dalam kekayaan maupun kemiskinan” merupakan hasil dari “legislasi positif”, yakni ketika hukum-hukum arbitrer menggantikan hukum alam dan “menciptakan monopoli serta privilese”. Dalam kapitalisme, menurut Spooner, pemilik modal memperoleh kekuasaan khusus dalam perekonomian—kekuasaan yang tidak ada hubungannya dengan kebebasan sederhana untuk memproduksi, bertukar, dan berkompetisi. Jika dilihat secara menyeluruh, intervensi negara pada akhirnya menguntungkan orang-orang kaya dan mereka yang memiliki koneksi politik, yakni elite ekonomi yang mempunyai akses khusus kepada mereka yang membuat dan menjalankan aturan yang harus kita semua patuhi.


Intervensi-intervensi tersebut memang tidak selalu sempurna, dan sistem kapitalisme monopoli di negara ini tentu dilapisi dengan berbagai kebijakan yang secara formal dimaksudkan untuk melindungi pekerja, konsumen, dan masyarakat miskin. Namun, tidak satu pun kebijakan tersebut mengubah tujuan mendasar intervensi negara: merampas hak para pemilik yang sah dan menempatkan massa masyarakat dalam posisi bergantung pada para pemberi kerja. Singkatnya, tujuan historis negara adalah perang kelas yang permanen, yakni penggunaan kekuasaan negara untuk melindungi sebuah kelas bangsawan sosial-ekonomi.


Karena itu, kaum kiri sebenarnya cukup tepat dalam persoalan ketimpangan, meskipun mereka cenderung keliru dalam memahami kebebasan, hak-hak individual, dan pasar. Kaum anarkis pasar menghendaki

keduanya

, kebebasan dan kesetaraan, dengan memperjuangkan masyarakat tanpa negara yang menjadikan kesetaraan dalam kebebasan dan otoritas sebagai hukum tertingginya.


Persaingan yang benar-benar terbuka merupakan kekuatan yang membubarkan sekaligus menyebarkan konsentrasi kekuasaan. Kaum libertarian seharusnya berhenti mencari-cari alasan untuk membenarkan ketimpangan yang luar biasa besar saat ini, seolah-olah kita sampai pada kondisi ini melalui

laissez-faire

 dan kedaulatan individu.


Seluruh hasil publikasi didanai sepenuhnya oleh donasi. Jika kalian menyukai karya-karya kami, kalian dapat berkontribusi dengan berdonasi. Temukan petunjuk tentang cara melakukannya di halaman Dukung C4SS:

https://c4ss.org/dukung-c4ss.

author: Daniel Hunter
title: Why we need to think outside the box this election
content:
This article

Why we need to think outside the box this election

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


This election is not like any other. You’ve heard that before, and so have I. But after decades of “this presidential election is the most important election in your lifetime,” I have finally conceded that this

midterm

 election may be the most important election in my lifetime — because it will be the ultimate test of whether Trump and MAGA have succeeded in their authoritarian consolidation of power. 


And so it’s appropriate that many groups are trying new things ahead of this election — because the old playbook alone won’t get us there.


No Kings.

 On Oct. 17, No Kings is going to try something it hasn’t tried before. Instead of another mass march, the coalition is holding

No Kings: Vote Early

, a

nonpartisan day of action

 in which communities will host block parties, BBQs and local protests to make a voting plan together and vote early where local rules allow. Organizers say it’s

“not purely a protest

,” but rather a nonpartisan action to encourage voter participation. The idea is to treat voting not as something we do alone, but as something we do together. I’m not old enough to remember it, but people used to go to the polls with their neighbors and make an event of it. This is bringing back that collective spirit.


(It’s easy to host. Go

here

 for all the info you need by Thursday Oct. 15.)


Election Holiday.

 Another experiment is popping up for the Nov. 3 election —

Election Day: Our Civic Holiday

. This group (which I’m a part of) rests on a simple idea: treating Election Day as a day for showing love for democracy by doing our civic duty. Vote, help someone else vote, become a poll worker or observer, or find another way to participate in civic life. The idea is to translate that into a cultural vibe, like Valentine’s Day, but for a different form of love — love for democracy and our neighbors.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


These are two experiments among many in how we protect elections in new ways under new circumstances. (I’ll be writing more about possible post-election actions later.) Neither solves the problem on its own, but both actions build on the understanding that stealing an election gets much harder when there’s a large blowout. Hungary is the reminder. As I

wrote in April

, Orbán’s defeat was so decisive that he conceded before all the votes were counted, with turnout

near 80 percent

, the highest since their transition to democracy. As Micah Sifry put it, it was “

too big to rig

.”


New tactics aren’t easy — and it’s worth reminding ourselves of that.


The trap of the winning tactic


Until now, No Kings has been known for one thing: enormous marches, each bigger than the last. Organizers

put the first at five million, the second at seven million, and the third, in March, at more than eight million

. When a tactic works like that, the pressure to keep repeating it is immense.


I’ve seen this up close. After Greta Thunberg began her Friday walkouts, Fridays for Future grew and grew. I was working with 350.org — a global environmental organization — at the time and we provided a lot of the backend technical support to help it grow. That growth created tremendous pressure and helped drive movement at the United Nations and in many countries. (You can certainly argue it contributed to the Inflation Reduction Act, which — despite significant cuts — has some parts that are still

very active

.)


But every tactic eventually peaks. As Saul Alinsky put it, “A tactic that drags on too long becomes a drag.” Suddenly an organization named for leaving school on Fridays needs to improvise — and that’s hard.


Student protesters asked me to write the

Climate Resistance Handbook

 to try to assist Fridays for Future (and others) to break out of their tactical doldrums.


Occupy Wall Street

 hit the same wall. In Philadelphia, where we had an encampment outside of City Hall, my ears still ring with painful, shouted debates over whether we could do anything other than occupy. The argument largely won out that occupying is the thing that held us together — and like most occupations around the country (but not all!), we never tactically transitioned.


That’s the pull: The familiar tactic feels like the glue. The drive to stay the course is strong. And it takes a strong decision-making process to …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

author: Jeremy Appel, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous rights at forefront of anti-AI data centre rally in ‘Edmonton’
content:
Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation speaks at an Oct. 3 rally against data centres outside the ‘Alberta’ legislature building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton).

Photo by Jeremy Appel


This story was originally published in

Alberta Native News

 on Oct. 6,

and appears here with permission and style edits

,

with added context from the author’s

earlier article

 from May 14

.


More than 100 people gathered outside the Legislative Assembly building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton) on Oct. 3 to protest the provincial and federal governments’ permissive approach towards building artificial intelligence data centres.  


Elder Taz Bouchier opened the rally with a land acknowledgement before tying the proposed 7.5-gigawatt Wonder Valley data centre near Grande Prairie’s potential water usage to the oil industry’s plans to release treated tailings fluids into the Athabasca watershed. 


“When did people lose sight of how valuable water is to living? When money came into play. That’s all these data centers are about,” said Bouchier. 


Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is challenging the province’s decision to award a water license of 24-million cubic metres to the Municipal District of Greenview for Wonder Valley without consulting the Treaty 8 First Nation, which relies on the Smoky River for its water. 


At the protest, Chief Sheldon Sunshine outlined a series of “very basic questions” he has for data centre proponents, including whether existing rules are sufficient “for the size and scale of what is being proposed” and whether there are sufficient water protections.


READ MORE:


AI data centers are booming. Indigenous People want help protecting their lands and knowledge


“What happens to our communities when these projects operate for decades?” Sunshine asked. “What happens to the land? What happens to the water? What happens to the wildlife? What happens to the air quality? What happens when multiple projects are operating in the same region? And perhaps most importantly, where is the assessment of the cumulative impacts?


“We can’t look at every project at one time and pretend the others don’t exist. We have to look at the whole picture.”


As first

reported

 by online news outlet

Canada’s National Observer

, Environment Alberta has exempted Wonder Valley from an environmental assessment. 


“Why are governments creating pathways to accelerate these developments before the public has confidence that the rules are strong enough? Why is the push happening so fast? What concessions are being made to attract these projects? Who negotiated those concessions?” asked Chief Sunshine. 


“Those are reasonable questions. Asking them does not make us anti-development. It makes us responsible.” 


He emphasized that he understands the government’s “economic strategy behind these projects,” in terms of attempting to create a new market for the province’s substantial natural gas resources. 


“But economic development cannot come at any cost,” said Sunshine. “You cannot build a new economy by putting the foundation of that economy on water that communities depend on, land that cannot be replaced, or an electrical system that people already rely on.


“You cannot call something responsible development simply because it creates jobs. Responsible development means understanding the consequences before you build.”


Edmonton-Strathcona NDP MP Heather McPherson opened her remarks by “acknowledging that Indigenous people in this country are on the front lines of this fight, and on the front lines of so many fights that we are being asked to fight as citizens right now,” referring to First Nations’

opposition

 to the province’s separatist movement. 


“We all owe Indigenous people in this province a debt of gratitude,” she added, “for being on the front line, protecting our sovereignty, protecting our climate, protecting our water and our land.”


READ MORE:


After court win, First Nations denounce ‘Alberta’ premier’s separation referendum plan


McPherson called it greatly “frustrating” that data centres are being fast-tracked while crucial community needs are being unmet. 


“We can’t build the homes that people need in this community, but we can build a data centre,” she said. “We can’t build clean water facilities for people in this country, but we can build a data center.


“The priority here for this government is to make billionaires wealthy at the expense of every single one of us here.”

author: subMedia
title: White Nationalists Off Secwépemc Territory
content:
There is a growing white supremacist genocide denial movement in so-called Canada.

On September 27th members of the Second Sons, a white nationalist militia, marched on unceded Secwépemc territory carrying racist banners near a former residential school where mass graves of Indigenous children were discovered.

This action was timed to occur three days before National Truth and Reconciliation Day a flawed and limited attempt to acknowledge Canada’s genocide of Indigenous peoples.

The Second Sons are tightly connected to the so-called ‘Active Clubs’ movement and have called to remove non-white people from Canada at gunpoint.

The Secwépemc have a long history of resistance to Canadian colonialism, including the Gustaffson Lake standoff in 1995, and more recently, the Tiny House Warrior movement, launched in resistance to the TransMountain Pipeline project.

White supremacy is inherent to settler colonialism.

Settler anarchists have a special responsibility to support Indigenous sovereignty and confront white nationalists wherever they rear their ugly heads.

Get together. Crew up. Confront white supremacy in all its forms.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

Morland encouraged fellow journalists to preserve their own work rather than discard it, explaining that materials that may seem unremarkable today can become valuable historical records. The archives offer researchers an opportunity to explore the experiences and contributions of women journalists and document the development of organizations such as JAWS.

The reception highlighted the importance of preserving women’s experiences in journalism, particularly as the profession continues to confront challenges. JAWS is helping ensure the future generations can study their work and understand the history of feminist media.

As Ms. approaches its 55th anniversary in December, marking 25 years with the Feminist Majority Foundation as publisher, the gathering celebrated the relationships, reporting and feminist organizing that have sustained the magazine and the broader movement. Speakers closed by celebrating Ms., Gloria Steinem, and the community of women journalists whose work continues to shape feminist media.

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas.


Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by


nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?


AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.  


When you meet someone with a workplace or tenant issue, the whole solidarity network takes on the demands of the case, with those with the grievance–the issue(s) they want to fight around that directly affects them–being core organizers of their own campaign. We use direct action tactics, which means we don’t go through the courts or ask the cops or nonprofits to take care of the situation for us; we rely on just us to get the demand met by putting pressure on the boss or landlord until it becomes so unbearable they have no choice but to give in.


Like most solidarity networks there is a small group of core organizers who respond to the day- to-day needs of the organization. The people with the demands must be a part of this group. Then, there is a larger membership which is involved in many of the functions of the organization, but not all of its functions. They may pass out flyers with us, make phone calls, or research campaign targets, for example. Then there is a much larger network of people who will come out to actions when called on.


BRRN: Walk us through how you started it. Why this kind of organization, and what kinds of fights do you take on?


AK:

 Our specific solidarity network wanted to take on wage theft campaigns as our main, but not exclusive, area of struggle. We began working with another organization here that works in immigrant communities around stopping deportations. They were getting a lot of calls about wage theft, and helped us start the solidarity network to meet this need. Most of our initial calls came directly from them, and our first campaign came out of one of these calls. We also understand that the immigrant community, especially here in Texas, is very vulnerable to wage theft, and they often feel they do not have a lot of options for getting back stolen wages. We want to change that! Eventually, we want to create a citywide network of people who can respond to wage theft grievances, and other workplace and housing issues. We want to make bosses and landlords scared to even think about messing with us! 


In ATX, we have a small and unorganized left with a larger activist scene. A solidarity network is one form of organization that can work well under these conditions because you really only need a handful of core organizers and access to lots of people to show up to actions. We also see this form of organization being one in which committed leftists can develop relationships with other members of the working class. We see a lot of the left in ATX being very insular and removed from other everyday people. We feel it is important to be organizing in working-class communities since it is us as a class that are capable of transforming society. 


We also want to help normalize direct action tactics to push our collective ability to struggle even further. Ultimately, we would like to see more working-class organizations in our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and more. The solidarity network isn’t meant to be

the form

 of organization for widespread worker rebellion, but it is one form of organization that can respond to specific conditions that …

title: French Youth Take the Streets against a Bleak Future : A Report
content:
This past week, thousands of teenagers have taken the streets of France, clashing with police as they demonstrate against the deplorable conditions in their high schools and a rapidly collapsing future. This is a promising sign, shifting attention from the seemingly unstoppable rise of the extreme right to the question of what people can do on a grassroots basis to defend themselves. Our correspondents in Paris explore the situation in detail.


Another unprecedented summer of record

heatwaves

,

droughts

, and

wildfires

 throughout Europe underlines the desperate situation we are all facing today, while politicians of all stripes and their techno-industrial sponsors continue to turn a blind eye, forcing us down the path to catastrophe in the name of progress.


Hoping to turn the page on these environmental disasters, the French government has hurriedly shifted focus to other priorities. The coming months represent a crucial transition for Emmanuel Macron and his government, as they will bring Macron’s second term to a close, opening a new political era in France. Candidates are already battling to succeed Macron in power at the beginning of May 2027.


In the midst of this political spectacle, during an increasingly

menacing surge

 in the popularity of the National Rally (formerly, the National Front), the extreme-right party, it is especially meaningful that teenagers have started to organize at a grassroots level to defend themselves. This organizing gained momentum last week, when blockades of high schools, demonstrations, and riots erupted across France, taking everyone by surprise.


Students clash with police forces in Montpellier on October 2, 2026.


Licensed to Kill?


Since Macron was elected President for the first time in May 2017, the political discourse in France has been even more dominated by an emphasis on authoritarian and far-right ideologies in terms of security, immigration, and economic and social issues.


This political shift towards an even more aggressive form of governance has led to increasing state violence targeting the social movements and uprisings that have emerged since. From the eviction of the

ZAD

 at Notre-Dame-des-Landes in 2017 to the

riots

 following the murder of Nahel in 2023, not forgetting the

Yellow Vest

 sequence and the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown experimental

doctrines

, we have experienced a headlong plunge into a world of surveillance, repression, and loss of individual freedoms. This has become today’s new normal.


It was in this already suffocating context that last July, the French government decided to vote on a new bill giving police officers more latitude to use their firearms without consequences—a demand that the far right has promoted for years. If voted through, this legislation could set a

dangerous precedent

, as it would establish “a presumption of ‘legitimate use of arms’ by police and gendarmes ‘in the exercise of their duty’.”


Police arrest a student in Lyons on October 1, 2026.


In other words, not only will police officers be able to freely use their weapons if in any situation they claim to fear for their lives or the lives of others, but authorities will no longer have to prove that the officers acted within the framework of the law, as they are required to do today. It will be up to the victims and their families to provide evidence that the use of firearms was not justified. We can already see how this new law represents a legislative tool enabling law enforcement agents, and therefore, the state, to cover up future murders.


Unwilling to let such a law pass without resistance, political opponents and radicals, who had rightly rebranded this law the “license to kill,” decided to organize massive demonstrations and events throughout France on the weekend of September 18 to 20.

Thousands

 of people took part in these protests in different major cities alongside traditional leftist politicians, rights groups such as Amnesty International and the League of Human Rights, and various lawyers and magistrates’ unions.


In the meantime, another call for action reusing all the codes of the Yellow Vest movement spread online. The origins of this call remain obscure, as some national

newspapers

 have raised the possibility that AI-generated accounts had flooded social media platforms with this rumor on purpose. Nevertheless, media and politicians began commenting on this potential resurgence of the Yellow Vest movement due to the …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. It is just fascinating to me that despite the fact that she has been in folklore for centuries, no new media has come out about her in years, and now these two instances pop up in the same year. Three, if you count the experimental film Báthory by Carlos Atanes. Something seems to be in the (bloody) water.

Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps The Blood Countess isn’t quite as gay as it could be. Then again, apparently Ottinger wrote the screenplay in 1998, almost 30 years ago, so that could potentially account for that. But still, I won’t say no to a lesbian vampire film so I’ll probably still check it out when it makes its North American theatrical release in spring 2027.

author: Ethieny Karen
title: Um quarto dos senadores que apoiam a PEC da Flexibilidade têm antepassados escravocratas
content:
A proposta que defende o fim da escala 6×1 sempre teve um contraponto: o argumento de que o trabalhador deva receber por horas trabalhadas e possa “negociar” diretamente com o patrão sobre como será sua jornada de trabalho.


Essa é a proposta central da chamada PEC da Flexibilidade, que foi apresentada pelo senador e coordenador de campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro à Presidência, Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), como uma alternativa ao fim da escala 6×1. Segundo o líder do PL na Câmara dos Deputados, Sóstenes Cavalcante (RJ), essa é a proposta que o candidato à presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro, deve defender mesmo se a PEC do fim da escala 6×1 for aprovada. “Na nossa mentalidade, nós nunca vamos mudar o conceito, a melhor relação é hora trabalhada, hora recebida”,

disse

 Sóstenes ao G1.


Críticos à PEC da Flexibilidade – entre eles, a própria deputada federal Érika Hilton, autora da proposta mais recente que defende o fim da escala 6×1 (

PEC 8/2025

) –

chamaram

 o projeto de “escravidão moderna” e “PEC da escravidão”.


A

Agência Pública

 apurou que dos

40 senadores

 favoráveis à PEC da flexibilização em maio, ao menos 10 têm antepassados diretos que foram donos de pessoas escravizadas ou se beneficiaram da escravidão. A proposta que flexibiliza a jornada de trabalho, bem como os salários,

está parada

 no Senado, mas sua tramitação pode ser retomada caso Flávio seja eleito.


Esse é o

caso

 dos antepassados do senador Rogério Marinho, mais especificamente do seu sétimo avô, o Capitão-mor Bento Freire, que viveu no Rio Grande do Norte entre 1727 e 1803. Segundo documentos analisados pela

Pública

, o capitão foi senhor de engenho e um rico proprietário de terras, e teria utilizado mão de obra de pessoas escravizadas.


A reportagem procurou o político para esclarecer os achados sobre sua árvore genealógica e a relação do antepassado com a escravidão, assim como fizemos com todas as autoridades citadas no

Projeto Escravizadores

, publicado em novembro de 2024. O senador não respondeu até a publicação do especial.


Já o senador Jayme Campos, que faz parte de uma das famílias mais poderosas e tradicionais na política mato-grossense. Tem como quinto avô Antonio José Pinto de Figueiredo, que foi um mestre de campo (patente militar da época, que hoje corresponde a posição de coronel), em Cuiabá.


E, segundo documentos, ele era dono de uma grande fazenda, composta de 83 escravos.


Em 2008, mais de dois séculos depois, 15 trabalhadores relataram condições degradantes de trabalho na fazenda Santa Amália, em Alta Floresta (MT), pertencente a Jayme Campos. Após as denúncias, o senador assinou um Termo de Ajustamento de Conduta com o Ministério Público do Trabalho na época para assinar a carteira de trabalho dos funcionários, garantir alojamento adequado, oferecer água potável e permitir descanso remunerado, entre outros.


Campos negou as irregularidades, disse que sofria perseguição política e que aceitou assinar o TAC porque “não tinha nada a temer”. Nós procuramos o político na época da publicação do

especial

, mas ele não respondeu.


A história se repete com outros nove senadores, veja a lista:


Efraim Filho (UNIÃO-PB)


O senador tem como tataravô Manoel De Araújo Pereira II. Registros indicam que ele teria possuído pessoas escravizadas em Santa Luzia, Paraíba, entre os anos de 1858 e 1888.


Tereza Cristina (PP-MS)


O tataravô da senadora foi Antonio Côrrea da Costa I, nascido em 1782 e falecido em 1854, no Mato Grosso. Segundo registros, ele herdou de seu pai o engenho Bom Jardim e, posteriormente, em 1805, adquiriu o engenho da Glória. Em 1821, tornou-se o segundo presidente da Província de Mato Grosso e, posteriormente, deputado. Em seus engenhos, produzia milho, arroz, feijão, açúcar e aguardente. Ele também teria possuído 8 mil cabeças de gado, 10 casas em Cuiabá e 194 pessoas escravizadas.


Marcos Pontes (PL-SP)


O sexto avô do senador foi o alferes Joaquim da Silveira Leite, nascido em 1758 no interior do estado de São Paulo e falecido em 1823. Oficial subalterno do corpo de milícias, ele era senhor de engenho, dedicando-se à produção de açúcar e aguardente. Segundo registros, o alferes teria possuído cerca de 10 pessoas escravizadas.


Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI)


O senador tem como tataravô o ex-presidente da província do Piauí por quatro mandatos, Simplício de Sousa Mendes, nascido em 1823 e falecido em 1892, e como quinto avô o tenente-coronel Antônio de Sousa Mendes, nascido em 1793 e falecido em 1871 …

author: Rizomatica
title: 83,000 hectáreas, 400 familias y 150 actores colectivos consolidan inclusión y participación relevante: Destacan al espacio costero (ECMPO) Mañihueico-Huinay
content:
La microserie «Zonas de Resguardo» estrenó su tercer capítulo sobre el ECMPO Mañihueico-Huinay, el espacio costero más extenso del sur de Chile, con 83.000 hectáreas, 400 familias y 150 convenios de uso. Por su parte, el geógrafo Álvaro Montaña destaca que la ley permite incluir a múltiples usuarios y genera un nuevo equilibrio de poder.


La ECMPO más grande del sur de Chile


El Espacio Costero Marino de Pueblos Originarios (ECMPO) Mañihueico-Huinay, en Hualaihué, es el más extenso del sur de Chile: 83.833 hectáreas de mar, 16 años de tramitación, decenas de organizaciones incluidas y 9.368 personas viviendo en su entorno. La Ley 20.249 permite que comunidades indígenas administren un espacio costero y que otras organizaciones locales participen como usuarios del mar, según establece el artículo 11. Pesca, choritos, algas, mariscos y turismo forman parte de la economía y la vida de Hualaihué, y la pregunta que surge es qué significa esto para el futuro del mar en Chile.


La inclusión como cambio de paradigma


Consultado al geógrafo Álvaro Montaña, quien desde Chiloé ha apoyado técnicamente algunos procesos de Espacios Costeros

, señala: «El artículo 11 de la ley que crea los espacios marinos costeros de pueblos originarios establece algo que es inédito en las figuras de administración territorial de la playa y el mar de Chile. Permite la inclusión. Si bien esta ley surge por una demanda de las comunidades indígenas y solo puede ser invocada por ellas, en la administración de los espacios marinos, las comunidades indígenas pueden integrar a otros usuarios. Juntas de vecinos, comités productivos, escuelas, centros de investigación, personas naturales, empresas, ya una serie de actores que se vinculan al uso y al manejo de los recursos del mar».


Montaña agrega que esto «sin duda genera un nuevo equilibrio de poder en la administración territorial de la playa y el mar porque transfiere poder a las comunidades locales, quienes hacen la gobernanza, toman las decisiones sobre el uso de sus espacios comunes». Y sostiene: «Este es, a mi juicio, uno de los aportes principales de la ley de los espacios costeros marinos de pueblos originarios porque permite esta inclusión de usuarios. Y a mi juicio, el espacio costero de Mañihueico-Huinay es un ejemplo, un modelo en el sur de Chile de cómo la ley de espacios costeros integra y da cabida a orilleros, pescadores, buzos, armadores y una serie de organizaciones sociales, culturales, ambientales y productivas que conviven a orillas del mar».


Vivir en una isla: la voz de Yohana Coñuecar


En el marco del tercer capítulo de la microserie

«

Zonas de Resguardo

«

, Yohana Coñuecar Llancapani,

destacada dirigenta, relata su experiencia: «Es algo que es muy difícil de explicar, pero muy fácil de sentir. Que esa relación con el mar en ningún rato se corta. Está ahí, constante, latiendo como la sangre, como del corazón». Yohana vive en la isla Llanchid, en la comunidad AdMapu kaLafken, en el espacio territorial de los Coñuecar Llancapani. «Vivir en una isla es único, así que los desafíos que implica vivir acá sean siempre constantes», dice.


«Nosotros dependemos del mar», afirma. «El hecho de vivir en una isla implica que tu única conexión con el mundo exterior es a través de la navegación. El hecho de que se pueda bajar a mariscar cuando quieras comer una cazuela de marisco, un curanto, no sé. Vas al mar, no vas al mercado, aquí vas al mar directo a buscar los recursos. Y además porque toda la gente de acá sabe dónde están los recursos. Dónde están las almejas, dónde están las chorras, dónde ir a buscar choritos, dónde ir a buscar piures, qué sé yo. Entonces hay un conocer constante de la gente de la isla sobre nuestro propio espacio».


Sobre el ECMPO, detalla: «El espacio costero Mañihueico-Huinay es un espacio costero de 83.833 hectáreas. Y como es un espacio costero como de fiordos, es el espacio costero más grande otorgado en el sur de Chile». Y agrega: «Este espacio costero reconoce a 150 actores, algunos individuales y otros más en organizaciones. Así que tiene una inclusión importante de pensamiento local. El uso de la habitabilidad habla en el fondo de un uso histórico de vivir cerca del mar. Que implica no solamente tener la casa cerca del mar, sino que es tener la casa y todos los elementos necesarios para vivir. Y eso que hoy día esté acreditado y puesto como un derecho, no nos habla solamente de un derecho presente, también habla de un derecho futuro».

author: Publicación Abierta
title: 12 de octubre: la conquista remata ahora la vida
content:
12 DE OCTUBRE: LA CONQUISTA REMATA AHORA LA VIDA


Por Rafael Bautista S.


La colonización ahora se propone


aniquilar al mundo entero, pues si no todos somos iguales,


la rebelión de las víctimas es el pecado


que hay que escarmentar,


porque dice Occidente: “toda la culpa la tienen las víctimas.


El verdugo es siempre inocente”.


Para los fines de la conquista, fue preciso, necesario y estratégico cercenar las memorias y ceremonias antiguas de los indios, porque en esos residuos de resistencia se reproducía su modo de vivir. La inversión religiosa la describe muy ben Guaman Poma de Ayala cuando señala que “les quitaron su ley antigua y les pusieron temor y culpa donde antes había justicia”. Para arrebatarles y despojarles de humanidad, no bastaba con reducirlos a la miseria sino acabar con su memoria y sus costumbres, con su historia y su cultura.


Pero lo que las armas habían pretendido terminar, sólo logró su aplazamiento, pues la memoria comenzó a renacer, una y otra vez que la amenaza del exterminio prendía sus terruños, pero también su rebeldía. Las armas jamás pudieron doblegar el espíritu de liberación que atravesó, hasta el día de hoy, todas las formas que adquirió la dominación, el despojo y el robo de su tierra sagrada.


Hoy la liberación se expresa como

restauración

. El “progresismo” no entiende que el progreso es un mito, que la alternativa ya no es aferrarse al tren del progreso sino ponerle un freno y proponerse, con mayor denuedo, despertar y

conservar

 los valores que la tradición de nuestros pueblos nos ha legado, frente al desastre y el desmoronamiento de los valores moderno-occidentales. Pero

restaurar

 no es volver sino

recrear

,

actualizar

 lo que hemos perdido: una existencia más digna, libre y justa, re-ligada a lo natural y espiritual, a la simpleza que significa vivir en plenitud; lejos del dinamismo, ritmo y la inclemencia del tiempo inhumano del capital y el mercado (una vida válida para todos, donde ya no gobierne la ambición de unos cuantos).


En el siglo XV, el Abya Yala estaba atravesando una época de esplendor civilizatorio, superior, en muchos casos, a la Cristiandad latino-occidental (porque Europa recién se estaba reconociendo como nueva entidad ontológica y geopolítica). En realidad, en 1492,

quien se descubre no es América sino Europa

 y lo hace no a partir del “encuentro” con el otro sino negando su humanidad, para afirmarse como superioridad absoluta, una vez que ha diezmado la capacidad de resistencia de los pueblos dominados. El Abya Yala no fue reducida civilizatoriamente por vivir en el atraso histórico, en la barbarie (que es una pura leyenda negra que está siendo desmentida, cada día, por los nuevos hallazgos y argumentos antropológicos, arqueológicos, demográficos, tecnológicos, etc., etc.).


No nos vencieron por astucia, inteligencia o superioridad sino por una incompatibilidad radical. La

cultura de la vida

 (en todas sus expresiones) respeta los límites éticos que manifiesta la idea del bien. Una cultura de muerte, basada en la culpa infinita, el sacrificio, la aniquilación del

humanismo del otro hombre

, no admite límite alguno. Como en la actualidad, cuando el Imperio y Occidente, en su decadencia, desatan la política del odio, desatan un poder sin límites. Salah ad-Dîn o Saladino lo expresaba así, refriéndose a los cruzados cristianos: es casi inhumano luchar contra ejércitos tan hambrientos de sangre y muerte. Si el monje Bernardo de Claraval estimulaba a los cruzados con el perdón de los pecados y el paraíso eterno, por cada moro que se aniquile, se comprende la crueldad que despierta el odio al “infiel”. Como hoy en Gaza, el Imperio y Europa jamás abandonaron esa brutalidad sin coordenadas morales. Los pueblos expulsados a ser periferia del “primer mundo”, fuera de las fronteras del

humanismo liberal-moderno excluyente y selectivo

, aun cargan con la interrogante: ¿cómo puede ser posible vivir en un mundo sin respeto por la vida?


Occidente nunca fue superior. Su moralidad los retrata en la figura de aquél que afirma que “lo único que puede detenerme es

Mi propia moral

,

Mi propio pensamiento

.

No necesito

 del derecho internacional”, Trump dixit. Occidente es el nicho de la tradición imperial, que siempre debe retornar, como dice Dostoievsky, al lugar del crimen. Es su condena y, por eso mismo, debe acallar a los vencidos, para dejar de escuchar el clamor de los muertos que deja su progreso y desarrollo.

title: Milei celebró el despido de los 920 trabajadores de FATE y se dio por reelecto en 2027
content:
El pasado domingo tuvo lugar el Festival por los trabajadores de Fate con bandas de heavy metal argentino de reconocida trayectoria y con la participación del Coro Nacional de Niños, para reclamar contra el cierre de la fábrica. El martes, el presidente Javier Milei aseguró estar «recontra convencido» de ganar las elecciones de 2027 y, con una frialdad estremecedora, defendió el cierre de la planta de FATE, la misma que dejó a 920 trabajadores y sus familias en la calle. P

or Infogremiales.


Mientras el Presidente fantasea con su reelección, la Justicia de San Isidro elevó a juicio oral a 24 trabajadores, entre ellos representantes sindicales nacionales, delegados y operarios, por la toma de la planta que mantienen desde febrero, cuando la patronal de Javier Madanes Quintanilla anunció el cierre definitivo y despidió a toda la plantilla.


«Se favorecen 48 millones, perdieron 920. La pregunta es: ¿esto es justo? Sabe por qué es justo, porque le estoy devolviendo libertad de que elija el neumático que usted quiera», argumentó Milei en diálogo con Radio Mitre. Teniendo en cuenta que baja el poder adquisitivo y el consumo, y que hasta el Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI) redujo drásticamente su proyección de crecimiento del PBI para la Argentina en 2026, llevándola del 3,5% al 2,1%, difícil comprender que destruir industria nacional sea realmente un buen negocio a largo plazo para los argentinos.


Desde febrero, los trabajadores sostienen esta ocupación temporaria como única herramienta para frenar el vaciamiento y exigir la reapertura de una fábrica que fue símbolo y única productora nacional de neumáticos durante 80 años. El SUTNA denunció desde el primer día que la paralización responde a un «lockout patronal ilegal», una figura que la empresa rechaza pese a que la planta está cerrada, las máquinas se desmantelan y los dueños se niegan a negociar. La respuesta del Estado viene siendo allanar el camino para el desalojo y, ahora, para la persecución penal de los trabajadores. «Pretenden, por medio de la persecución y el hostigamiento judicial, poner fin a una lucha justa contra un ilegal lockout patronal», denunció el gremio.


La escalada represiva no se detiene. En septiembre, la Sala II de la Cámara de Apelaciones y Garantías de San Isidro ordenó el desalojo de la planta, una medida que fue suspendida tras el recurso presentado por el SUTNA, pero que se mantiene latente sobre los trabajadores. Ahora, la Justicia avanzó un paso más y elevó a juicio oral a los 24 trabajadores, en una causa que el sindicato calificó como «totalmente aberrante» y que, en los hechos, equipara a los trabajadores que defienden su fuente laboral con delincuentes comunes. La CTA Autónoma y la CGT ya habían respaldado al SUTNA y reclamado el levantamiento del lockout, pero el Poder Judicial, lejos de escuchar ese reclamo, decidió avanzar con la criminalización.


Mientras Milei se jacta de su «billetera» de 125.000 millones de dólares y de su confianza en la reelección, el conflicto de FATE, que ya lleva más de siete meses, no aparece en su agenda ni en sus discursos más que para señalar a los 920 trabajadores despedidos como una especie de «mal necesario» y un supuesto beneficio para el resto de los argentinos. Una declaración extraña teniendo en cuenta que el país pierde con el cierre de FATE a la única fábrica nacional de neumáticos. En cambio, sí hubo respaldo a las críticas contra el empresario dueño de la fábrica, pero no para defender a los trabajadores, sino para dirimir una interna entre el Presidente Milei y Madanes Quintanilla por el acuerdo con Estados Unidos y los aranceles al aluminio.


En paralelo, el domingo 11 desde las 11 de la mañana, los trabajadores de FATE armaron un festival de bandas de heavy metal nacionales en el predio del SUTNA Pilar. Contaron con el acompañamiento de 13 bandas como Horcas, Tren Loco, Lázaro, entre otras, y la participación especial del Coro Nacional de Niños, bajo la consigna «FATE no se cierra».

author: Darío Aranda
title: "Debemos cuidar el hogar que habitamos, el hogar-cuerpo, el hogar-tierra"
content:
Por Sergio Sánchez


Pablo Bruno creció entre un barrio popular de la capital cordobesa y el paisaje de las sierras. Oriundo del barrio General Pueyrredón, el joven cantante, guitarrista y compositor pateó las agitadas calles de su ciudad y conectó tempranamente con la fuerza vital de la naturaleza. “También crecí en el barrio Centro América, que es donde vivían mis abuelos. Fueron los dos lugares donde me he criado, unas raíces bien cordobesas”, resalta el músico de 28 años. “Siempre estábamos en la calle con la changada, andando en bicicleta, jugando a la pelota, echando moco. Agradezco esa niñez, porque la pude disfrutar”, dice. “Además, mis viejos desde chiquitito siempre me llevaron a las Sierras Chicas de Córdoba. Empecé a ir desde los 4 años para allá y le agarré amor al monte. En paralelo, con mis abuelos íbamos siempre al campo”, recuerda.


“Entonces, el barrio, las sierras y el campo fueron los tres lugares a donde me crie”, sintetiza Bruno, quien acaba de publicar su cuarto disco de estudio,

Hogar

 (2026), una obra que justamente habla de cuidar la casa propia: la íntima y la social; la espiritual y la comunitaria.


"Entré en el vuelo de la palabra hogar como filosofía. Lo más importante que podemos hacer es

cuidar ese hogar que habitamos, ese hogar-cuerpo, ese hogar-tierra

, que es lo mismo", grafica el cantautor antes de presentar el disco el viernes 16 de octubre a las 21 en JJ Circuito Cultural (Jean Jaures 347). "

En las canciones está ese cuidado hacia la sierra, la naturaleza, que es el lugar más presente que tenemos para habitar y cuidar

. Hace unos días venía de Mendoza, de San Rafael, y un amigo me decía: 'Nosotros estamos defendiendo el agua'. Más allá de la palabra lucha, porque es una defensa que tenemos que realizar como tribu para las nuevas generaciones".


Con el acento puesto en la música de raíz folklórica, el disco recorre diferentes estados emocionales y climas musicales, desde la cumbia "Luna de los desvelos" hasta la introspectiva y despojada "Sentirme hogar", pasando por la chacarera percusiva "Donde el milagro hecha brotar", la reflexiva "Zamba del juglar", la instrumental “Canción de otoño” o la chacarera comunitaria "Ahicito en los encuentros".


Foto: Prensa Pablo Bruno


“Encontrarnos, compartir el pan/ construir en hermandad/ Volvamos a lo simple/ militemos la paz/ Donde el amor construye/ un puente al hogar”, canta como un manifiesto de vida en “El abrazo de hogar”.

"En la comunidad entra la familia, las amistades, la tribu con la que uno comparte y la naturaleza

; el sitio que uno elige vivir y cuidar", sostiene el artista en torno al concepto.


—

¿De dónde nace tu necesidad de defender el monte, el agua y las sierras?


—En las Sierras Chicas he compuesto más de la mitad de mis canciones. Es un lugar donde no llega el agua, estuve viviendo un tiempo ahí. Hay todo un sistema de riego y cuando llueve se llenan los tanques. Entonces, la lluvia está relacionada con la bendición. Uno cuando no tiene el agua se da cuenta de la importancia y la vitalidad máxima que tenemos. Uno aprende a habitar una conciencia del cuidado. En Córdoba estamos muy acostumbrados a gente que lava los platos y deja la canilla abierta. Y hay sitios donde el agua falta.


—

¿Y una canción puede ser un instrumento o herramienta para despertar una reflexión?


—Hace unos días estaba cantando una canción inédita en San Rafael, que en un momento dice: "Agua tesoro del mundo". También dice: "Vivo feliz cantando/ con la esperanza firme en la canción". Creo que desde el arte, en este caso desde la música, es sumamente importante poner en palabras ciertas cuestiones, porque la gente siempre se sensibiliza más a través del arte. Porque toca células más sutiles. Y va a despertar algo a través de una canción, una poesía o una obra de teatro. El arte siempre es fundamental para habitar esos espacios. Estamos atravesando un presente particular en relación a

la lucha por el agua

. Y en Mendoza le están poniendo el cuerpo a esa causa hace mucho tiempo.


—

¿Sentís una responsabilidad social de hablar sobre determinados temas que te incomodan en esta época?


—Lo siento algo muy personal y de búsqueda artística. Es importante cantarle a lo que veo en cuanto a injusticias o maltrato hacia la naturaleza. O sobre otras cosas, como cantar hacia adentro de uno mismo. Habitar esos lugares implica una responsabilidad muy linda. No me sale cantar por cantar. Siento que cobra sentido cuando hay una palabra a la …

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.
