title: Europa Zapatista. Dos Pronunciamientos: “La Casa y la Escuela”
content:
Dos Pronunciamientos: “La Casa y la Escuela” La Casa

No fue la foto de una mujer de 87 años, expulsada de su hogar de toda la vida, a la que sacaron de su casa en una camilla camino del hospital, la que rompió el muro por el que se desbordó la indignación. Fueron las imágenes que estaban dentro de esa imagen: familias expulsadas de sus casas porque los alquileres han subido tanto que no pueden pagarlos; hombres, mujeres, niños, expulsados de sus barrios, porque las élites financieras e inmobiliarias han decidido que las ciudades no son para vivir, sino el escenario teatral por el que circulen los turistas y compren, sobre todo compren, cualquier cosa, desde baratijas a modo de recuerdo, hasta cantidades ingentes de alcohol, paseando sus penurias por calles antes llenas de vida, de la vida de la gente que las habitaba.

No fue el nombre y la voz de Maricarmen, diciendo a las personas que, unas pocas horas antes de ser expulsada del lugar que llevaba habitando 70 años, estaban en la calle intentando impedir su desahucio, que siguieran luchando, no por ella, sino por todos, por todas, por una vivienda digna, por una ciudad habitable y por obligar a que se garantice el derecho de todos los ciudadanos a disfrutar de una vivienda digna y adecuada, mensaje que repitió después, ya desde el hospital. Fueron los nombres y las voces que están dentro del nombre de Maricarmen: Manuela, Andrés, Rosa, Ibrahim, Candela, Antonio, Rawda, Miguel, Emily, Nicolás y así hasta nombrar a los miles que perdieron sus casas sin tener ni un lugar digno dónde refugiarse; algunos, incluso perdieron la vida junto a la casa, porque no se veían viviendo y durmiendo a la intemperie.

No fueron solo los expulsados de sus casas, que es como decir de sus vidas; fue también la imposibilidad de tantos, de tantas, de conseguir una vivienda digna y asequible, de tener la posibilidad de vivir, de tan solo vivir. Fue la intranquilidad diaria de quienes hoy por hoy tienen un techo, pero no saben si lo tendrán mañana, porque igual conservarlo va a significar quedarse sin recursos para vivir la vida.

Las plazas se han llenado de tiendas de campaña, como imagen de un futuro que, de una forma u otra, nos alcanzará, como la imagen del único lugar en que podremos refugiarnos: la calle sin techo; solo que esta vez, esa última oportunidad de refugio se ha plantado en mitad de su escenario teatral, y ahora lo ve todo el mundo. Las acampadas en las plazas de un buen puñado de ciudades españolas, son al tiempo una denuncia y una recuperación del espacio para lo que siempre tuvo que ser, un lugar de encuentro entre personas, iguales y diferentes, que se ven, que se escuchan y se comparten.

En 1976, recién muerto el dictador Franco, el por entonces vicepresidente y ministro de Gobernación, Manuel Fraga, que años antes fue ministro en la dictadura, quiso evitar la celebración en las calles del primer Primero de Mayo en libertad, diciendo en voz alta lo que los “mandones” del poder económico y político pensaban antes y piensan ahora: “la calle es mía”. Pero no, la calle nunca fue suya, la calle es de todos, de todas, de todoas; la calle es el encuentro, la libertad, la lucha… Y las acampadas en las plazas son por todo eso, resumido en una vivienda justa, en la Vida y en la Dignidad.

Nota: Maricarmen murió en el hospital, catorce días después de ser desahuciada.

title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?

author: Andrea DiP
title: Em Israel, conferência da extrema direita exalta Flávio Bolsonaro
content:
Nos dias 06, 07 e 08 de outubro, a cidade de Jerusalém sediou a “National Conservatism Conference”, ou “NatCon” (algo como Conferência sobre Conservadorismo Nacional), evento que reúne algumas vezes ao ano políticos conservadores nacionalistas de extrema direita da Europa, Estados Unidos, Israel, Reino Unido e, algumas vezes, da América Latina.


Mas digamos que nossa região não é tão importante para eles, a não ser quando se fala contra a imigração de “países pobres” – nestes casos, os discursos nos colocam como quintal dos Estados Unidos, ou interessam a alianças que podem servir às suas causas. Sei disso porque já participei de outra NatCon em Bruxelas em 2024 e tenho me infiltrado nesses eventos transnacionais da extrema direita europeia desde 2022.


A NatCon é financiada pela Fundação estadunidense Edmund Burke, que tem entre seus principais doadores a Heritage Foundation. A Heritage Foundation, por sua vez, é uma das principais geradoras de diretrizes políticas para a atual administração Trump. Seu presidente, Kevin Roberts, descreve explicitamente a missão moderna da Heritage Foundation como a de “institucionalizar o Trumpismo” em uma

entrevista

 para o New York Times. Roberts foi um dos palestrantes da conferência em Jerusalém. E a Heritage está de olho no Brasil: em março deste ano, Paulo Figueiredo e Alexandre Ramagem

participaram

 de um evento da fundação em Miami, como revelou a

Pública

.


Eu estava lá nesta edição da NatCon, que reuniu políticos israelenses de extrema-direita, figuras europeias que enfrentaram medidas disciplinares por suposto antissemitismo e figuras nacionalistas cristãs e de extrema-direita dos Estados Unidos, como bem definiu o jornal britânico

The Guardian

. 


O foco principal estava no apoio às políticas e medidas de Benjamin Netanyahu contra os palestinos, a defesa do Estado de Israel, da conquista de territórios na Cisjordânia e na celebração e endosso de ações dos colonos israelenses que agem como uma milícia na região, cometendo todo tipo de barbaridades, como contei um pouco

na minha última coluna

. Também foram defendidas ações “anti-terrorismo” e anti-imigração na Europa e Estados Unidos e o combate ao que foi chamado de “red green alliance” (aliança verde e vermelha), que é como a extrema direita tem se referido à parte da esquerda progressista que protesta contra o genocídio do povo palestino. Uma das principais referências dessa aliança seria, na visão destes radicais, o prefeito de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani. Alguns palestrantes também atacaram ferrenhamente a comunidade LGBTQIA+, sobretudo as pessoas trans, e falaram da importância de criar grandes famílias, ter muitos filhos, mas sem se misturar com pessoas de diferentes culturas.


Um dos discursos mais violentos veio de Sebastian Gorka, subchefe de gabinete do presidente e diretor sênior de contraterrorismo no Conselho de Segurança Nacional dos Estados Unidos, que participou ao vivo e online da Casa Branca. Gorka é um dos aliados de Eduardo Bolsonaro nos EUA, a quem

foi apresentado

 por Steve Bannon.


Ele defendeu que existe hoje uma nova religião: “a religião da esquerda”.


“Seja ela preenchida por ambientalistas adoradores de Gaia como Greta Thunberg, seja pelo altar do DEI (Diversidade, Equidade e Inclusão, em inglês)”, disse. Seu discurso misturou a Irmandade Muçulmana com marxismo, se estendeu para ligações entre o Hamas, e a “mã do Irã”. “A Aliança Vermelho-Verde é real. Os islamistas trabalhando com os marxistas é real”. E finalizou parafraseando Trump: “Se você planeja machucar americanos ou matar inocentes, nós vamos encontrar você e nós vamos matar você”.


Foi neste clima de Conferência que o nome de Flávio Bolsonaro foi citado e aplaudido pelos presentes – cerca de 300 pessoas.


O europarlamentar Harald Vilimsky, que lidera a delegação do Partido da Liberdade da Áustria (FPÖ) no Parlamento Europeu e atua como vice-presidente do grupo “Patriotas pela Europa”, foi quem levantou a bola:


“Quero que a Europa fique ombro a ombro com Israel, com aqueles que, em termos de fé, são nossos irmãos mais velhos. Quero a parte conservadora dos Estados Unidos em nosso campo, não os Republicanos apenas no nome, mas os verdadeiros conservadores. Isso é algo que realmente poderia ser um divisor de águas no desenvolvimento internacional. Quero a Argentina com o presidente Javier Milei em nossas fileiras. Quero o Chile com o Presidente José Antonio Kast ao nosso lado. Quero Flávio Bolsonaro no Brasil.” …

author: Unknown
title: Kurdish Conference at European Parliament Begins with reception: Abdullah Öcalan must be released
content:
The 20th conference, organized by the European Union Turkey Civic Commission (EUTCC) and patronized by Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Iranian human rights advocate Shirin Ebadi, human rights activist Bianca Jagger, and Kurdish politician Leyla Zana, recipient of the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, began with a reception.


The reception, held at the European Parliament on the evening of 14 October, was attended by numerous people, including Pervin Buldan, a member of the Imralı Delegation; European parliamentarians such as Shirin Ebadi, Martin Schirdewan, Andreas Schieder, and Leoluca Orlando; politicians and activists such as Hisyar Özsoy and Sebahat Tuncel; and lawyer Raziye Öztürk of the Asrın Law Office, representing the legal community. The conference will continue tomorrow, 15 October.


The 20th conference marks a turning point


Opening the reception, Dersim Dağdeviren, a member of the EUTCC Board and affiliated with Kurd-Akad, said the 20th conference marked a turning point for the EUTCC. “At the same time, it is an opportunity to pause and ask ourselves: What have we achieved? What have we failed to accomplish? And, most importantly, what responsibility do we bear for the future?” he said.


Noting that the EUTCC had spent two decades providing a space for critical dialogue on relations between the European Union and Türkiye, the Kurdish question, democracy, human rights, and the pursuit of peace, Dersim Dağdeviren said: “There is a motto that captures our collective work in a special way: When one person dreams, it is only a dream. When many people dream together, it is the beginning of a new reality.”


International support is necessary for the process to succeed


Dersim Dağdeviren said that this reality was reflected in the 20-year history of EUTCC conferences held at the European Parliament. He then drew attention to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey.


Describing it as an important opportunity to resolve the Kurdish question on a political basis, Dersim Dağdeviren said: “A successful process cannot be sustained solely through the efforts of the parties directly involved. It also requires sustained international support. The European Union and its member states must actively support dialogue, encourage talks between the parties, and create the political conditions necessary for a lasting, democratic solution.”


Shirin Ebadi: Abdullah Öcalan must be released


Nobel laureate and lawyer Shirin Ebadi then addressed the gathering in Persian, greeting Öcalan and stating: “Abdullah Öcalan has shown the courage necessary for peace and must be released. I demand the immediate and unconditional release of Abdullah Öcalan.”


Adding that “the courage Abdullah Öcalan has demonstrated shows that he deserves to be one of the pioneers of the peace process,” Shirin Ebadi continued: “In my view, the time has now come for him to be freed. I see this platform as an opportunity to call for Abdullah Öcalan’s release without any preconditions.


The Kurds have the capacity to pursue their struggle through a political party in Turkey and to continue fighting for democracy and their legitimate rights. They can secure their rights within Turkey’s borders through democratic politics. Believe me, this is the path that will enable you to achieve your goals more effectively. My wish is for all ethnic groups in Turkey and elsewhere in the world, including Iran, to enjoy human rights and the right to live as equals, free from discrimination.”


Schirdewan said Europe must address two issues, Palestine and Kurdistan


Martin Schirdewan, a Member of the European Parliament and Co-Chair of The Left group, said: “As European lawmakers, we can develop a better understanding of what is needed to achieve lasting peace in Kurdistan and the Middle East.”


The co-chair of The Left added: “We also believe there are two fundamental issues that European politicians need to address. First, there is the issue of Palestine. We need to discuss a Palestinian state and the right of the Palestinian people to statehood. Second, there is the issue of the Kurds’ national status and their right to determine their own future.


Ultimately, it is up to you to decide what you want. What we can do, and what we can offer you, is support in building a society founded on democracy and equality. You must make the decision, not someone else. No one who oppresses the Kurdish people should make that decision …

author: Kodao Productions
title: Mary Grace Piattos: The Mystery Sara Duterte and Marcos Jr. Cannot Escape
content:
Mary Grace Piattos may remain a mystery forever in the Sara Duterte impeachment trial. With the withdrawal of Article I, the Senate may never determine who received the money acknowledged under that name or where it went.


But the bigger question is why the search for answers should stop here, when the confidential funds in question were allocated in 2022, under the Marcos-Duterte political alliance, while Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte were still close allies.


The controversy is not just about an unexplained name on a receipt. It is about millions of pesos in public funds, the officials who handled them, and the government that allocated them.


Duterte must answer for the use of funds entrusted to her offices. Marcos, for his part, cannot simply distance himself from the allocation made under his administration. His specific responsibility for the approval and oversight of those funds deserves scrutiny, even as any personal liability must be established by evidence.


Mary Grace Piattos may be a mystery, but the responsibility for the money must not be


This is the gravely troubling consequence of Day 39 of the impeachment trial. After 38 days of presenting witnesses and documentary evidence on four articles of impeachment, the House prosecution panel withdrew three charges and decided to concentrate on Article II, involving Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth, questionable Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), and alleged failure to divest from business interests.


Lead prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro defended the move, saying the remaining charge was strong enough to stand on its own and that concentrating on it would shorten the proceedings.

“All-in po tayo dito,”

 she declared.


There may be a tactical justification for narrowing the case. But an impeachment trial is not merely a race toward conviction. The question is whether a faster verdict is worth leaving other serious allegations unresolved.


By withdrawing Articles I, III, and IV, the prosecution abandoned the opportunity for the Senate to rule on allegations involving confidential-fund misuse, bribery and corruption, and grave threats against Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and House Speaker Martin Romualdez. Only Article II will proceed.


While the withdrawal neither establishes guilt nor amounts to an acquittal, it does, however, leave three sets of allegations without a determination on their merits in this impeachment proceeding.


The public is entitled to ask why charges originally considered serious enough to include in the articles of impeachment are now being abandoned and what other avenues remain for investigating them.


This concern is straightforward: the choice of which charges to pursue should not determine which allegations of abuse of public power are ultimately examined.


Article I brought the confidential and intelligence funds handled by the OVP and the DepEd during Duterte’s tenure into public scrutiny. Audit records, bank transactions, liquidation reports, and testimony from government auditors and other officials raised questions about acknowledgment receipts, unusual cash withdrawals, and the documentation used to account for public money.


Mary Grace Piattos became the most memorable symbol of those questions. With Article I withdrawn, the Senate – and the public in general – will no longer determine whether the evidence presented under that charge supports a finding of fraudulent liquidation or other wrongdoings.


The investigation must therefore continue through the Commission on Audit, the Office of the Ombudsman, and other competent authorities, as appropriate to their respective mandates. The withdrawal of an impeachment charge is not a clearance of the transactions under scrutiny.


Confidentiality may be necessary for legitimate intelligence operations, but it cannot excuse questionable liquidation or inadequate documentation. These funds come from taxpayers, and the secrecy surrounding them makes credible independent oversight indispensable.


Without effective controls, as it is now, billions in confidential and intelligence funds are becoming a pork barrel for powerful officials, beyond meaningful public scrutiny.


Marcos Jr Cannot Distance Himself from the Allocation


The 2022 confidential funds allocation must also be examined in the context of the political alliance between Marcos and Duterte. They ran together, governed together, and occupied the …

author: groundxero
title: A Ledger of Crime, or a Ledger of Power? Reading West Bengal’s Latest Crime Figures
content:
West Bengal’s latest crime figures are being wielded as political ammunition. But the gap between crimes committed and crimes recorded raises a deeper question: whose suffering does the state choose to count?


 


by

 Tinku Khanna


 


For the past few days, an image has been circulating on WhatsApp and Facebook under a large headline announcing an “explosion of crime” in West Bengal since the BJP government took office in May. Beneath it is a table drawn from a Right to Information (RTI) reply attributed to the State Crime Records Bureau (SCRB): between 1 May and 24 September 2026, a span of 147 days, the state recorded 600 murders, 13,114 attempts to murder, 2,454 rapes and 32,341 cases of assault causing grievous hurt. An English-language news report carrying the same figures, in a more measured tone, is circulating alongside it. We added up every monthly figure in both, and the arithmetic is sound.


 


The RTI application was filed by Saket Gokhale, a Trinamool Congress leader and former Rajya Sabha MP, and the party published the figures on 7 October under the banner “2,400+ rape cases in Bengal in just 5 months under BJP”. The BJP’s response, through its spokesperson Debjit Sarkar, was that many of these cases concern offences committed under the previous government: delayed complaints, including those of rape and post-poll violence, were registered only after the change of government. The date on which each offence occurred, Sarkar argued, should therefore be checked before anyone speaks of a crime trend. Read together, the two parties have made the central argument of this essay without meaning to. One is brandishing a ledger that its own police kept thin for fifteen years; the other is admitting that the ledger is now swollen with crimes that were never written down.


 


The problem lies elsewhere. An “explosion” is a claim about change, a statement that something is now far larger than it used to be, and neither document says what it used to be. Once these figures are placed beside the state’s own earlier record, the picture that emerges is far less simple than the headline, and far more troubling in a different way.


 


The argument of this essay is an uncomfortable one: in West Bengal, crime statistics have long been less a measure of crime than a measure of power. Whether a complaint becomes a case is decided at the police station, and in this state the police have always moved to the rhythm of whoever governs. Under the Trinamool Congress, the ledger was suspiciously thin; in five months under the new government it has suddenly swollen. Both deserve the same suspicion, and at the centre of that suspicion should stand the women whose names never make it into any government’s ledger at all.


 


II


 


Anyone who works with crime statistics knows why murder is treated as the most reliable figure in the set: a body is hard to hide, a post-mortem is mandatory, and a police station has very little room to refuse a case. If violence in a state has genuinely surged, murders should rise with it. Murder is, in that sense, the control variable against which every other category can be read.


 


By the SCRB’s own figures, the state has averaged about four murders a day under the new government, roughly 124 a month or 1,490 a year. In 2023, the NCRB recorded 1,686 murders in West Bengal, about 140 a month. Murder has not exploded; it has fallen by roughly 12 per cent.


Figure 1. Annualised pace of reported cases in West Bengal in 2026 compared with earlier official figures.


Note: The 2026 figures are annualised estimates based on the SCRB totals for 1 May–24 September 2026. The grievous-hurt comparison is between West Bengal’s annualised pace and the all-India total for 2023; it is not a like-for-like comparison.


 


Now look at the other two rows. The NCRB recorded 1,110 rapes in West Bengal in all of 2023; the SCRB records 2,454 in fewer than five months. The grievous-hurt figure is stranger still. At the current pace, the state would register around 80,000 such cases a year, against 99,588 for the whole of India in 2023. A single state does not, in the space of a season, begin to account for four-fifths of the country’s serious assaults while its murder rate holds steady. That is not the signature of rising violence. It is the signature of a change in what is being counted, or in what the police are now willing to write down.


 


Which of these it is, we cannot say, because the SCRB has not …

title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Six years on, a mother grieves death of son killed in the ‘drug war’
content:
Lorna Carina Pepaño. Screengrab from the Philippine Truth Commission

“For me, justice and healing mean holding accountable those who carried out the killings, the perpetrators, those who gave the orders, and the highest-ranking officials behind the killings.”

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Seeing her son’s body, his blood spilling in the streets, Lorna Carina Pepaño could not cry. That day, on May 18, 2020, her son Christian was shot dead by two unidentified men while buying medicines and coffee for Pepaño.

On the day of the incident, Pepaño ran to the scene of the crime without slippers. Many of the witnesses she talked to said that Christian was begging for his life, telling the perpetrators that he was not the person they were after. The witnesses also heard one of the gunmen saying that Christian was not the target.

Six years later, Pepaño mustered the courage to tell the story of her son during the fourth public truth-telling session organized by the independent Philippine Truth Commission on October 9, 2026.

“All I feel until now is anger,” Pepaño said in Filipino. “Back then, I was shouting, saying words I never thought I could say. Never did I think that my son would be killed that day. I have so many questions but not a single answer.”

The police medico-legal report revealed that Christian died of four gunshot wounds in the head and trunk. The manner of death was also specified as homicide. All four gunshot wounds were fatal, causing immediate death.

“I could not sleep (properly) for five months. I was only drinking coffee. My grandson was also deeply affected by the incident. He would wake up shouting in the middle of the night,” Pepaño added.

Pepaño deeply misses his son. Christian only finished primary school because he took care of his grandmother in the province in the early years of his life, while Pepaño was a security guard in Manila.

The year Christian was killed was supposed to be his 40th year. On his 39th birthday, Pepaño prepared a small feast and a gift – a smartphone – for Christian. It was the first birthday celebration they organized as a family because that was the only time Pepaño could afford it.

“It was his happiest birthday. We rented a videoke and he sang his heart out. He hugged me and thanked me for the celebration,” Lorna said. “I never thought that it would be his last birthday celebration.”

Forensic pathologist Raquel Fortun, who is also a Commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, conducted an autopsy of Christian’s body on February 15, 2024, almost four years after he was summarily killed. She confirmed the two gunshot wounds in the head, but could not confirm the two gunshot wounds in the trunk since the body was already in advanced decomposition and they could only recover bones.

“Christian was in a really bad shape with the fatal shots in the head alone,” said Fortun, noting that all wounds were sutured based on the police medico-legal report. “There is no full homicide investigation. We do not have scene documentation.”

The bottom line, she emphasized, is that killings continue during the administration of Rodrigo Duterte, because there is no proper investigation.

More than 30,000 were extrajudicially-killed during the Duterte administration, according to the report of independent human rights groups. Only five cases resulted in conviction, as monitored by the Philippine Truth Commission, while some remain on appeal.

The fourth truth-telling session happened a day after the International Criminal Court (ICC) released the public redacted version of the decision, declaring that Duterte is fit to stand trial based on the assessment of independent medical experts. The ICC also adopted measures for his participation in his trial, which is slated to start on November 30 this year.

“Christian’s case was not part of the ICC. We call that temporal jurisdiction. The ICC is limited to the crimes committed from 2011 to 2019, the temporal limitation does not apply to the Truth Commission,” former ICC Judge Raul Pangalangan, chairperson of the Philippine Truth Commission, said in a press conference.

He emphasizes that there are differences in the mandate of the Philippine Truth Commission and the ICC. The former is not limited to temporal jurisdiction or the timeframe when the Philippine government was a member-state of the ICC. But their main objective was to provide a platform for the victims to share their stories.

author: rti_admin
title: Her life ended in one night. Her justice is still in the queue
content:
“Who will answer?” And “We cheered because the courts made us wait!”

Every rape case begins with a person: a daughter, a sister, a mother who trusted the road home. The numbers can feel cold, but they are made of lives, and any honest conversation has to carry both the data and the grief.

In November 2025, the World Health Organization and its UN partners released their most comprehensive estimates yet on violence against women (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240116962). Approximately 840 million women, nearly one in three, have experienced partner or sexual violence in their lifetime, and the rate has barely changed in 25 years (https://www.who.int/news/item/19-11-2025-lifetime-toll–840-million-women-faced-partner-or-sexual-violence). For the first time the report also estimated sexual violence by someone other than a partner: approximately 263 million women have experienced it since age 15 (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/violence-against-women). Experts caution that this figure is significantly under-reported because of stigma and fear (https://www.who.int/news/item/19-11-2025-lifetime-toll–840-million-women-faced-partner-or-sexual-violence).

Behind “under-reported” are women who stayed silent because they feared blame, and families who chose “honour” over justice. Prevention gets almost nothing. Only 0.2% of global development aid in 2022 went to programmes that prevent violence against women, and funding has fallen further since 2025.

Daayra is a 2026 crime thriller co-written and directed by Meghna Gulzar, released in theatres on 18 September 2026, inspired by true events in which a young woman disappears from a highway. Her family goes to the police, but they do not take the case seriously. The next day, her body is found on a deserted stretch, and the case dominates the headlines. The four accused, including one juvenile, are arrested and shot dead before they can be produced in court. The country rejoices, while others allege the encounter was staged.

Reviewers describe two philosophies at the centre: One believes capital punishment is the best solution. The other believes in social upliftment, teaching people consent and boundaries.

Some critics felt the film plays it safe and takes no clear stand, though they credit it with the potential to generate discussion.

When people cheer the deaths of the accused, the easy reading is bloodlust. The harder and more honest reading is exhaustion.

While Daayra plays in theatres, Delhi is living its own version. On September 21, 2026, a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped at a park near Delhi’s Kalkaji area. (https://www.newsgram.com/delhi/2026/09/28/miranda-house-students-protest-ground-report-kalkaji-rape-case-1). A birthday, a temple, a walk in a park turn into something worse than a nightmare. The case has been registered under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the POCSO Act, and the police arrested all three accused. Followed by a march on September 28th organized by Miranda House students.

Why should the classroom go online? Why should the campus be emptied, the gate avoided, the evening cancelled, the dupatta pulled tighter, and the phone kept in hand? Why is it always her world that gets smaller after a crime that was never hers?

We tell our daughters, sisters, mothers….to be careful. We never ask anyone to teach their progeny to be safe, irrespective of gender. We call it “protection,” but it is a curfew placed on the wrong people.

One protester said the country has endured this for years because we keep saying, “Koi Baat Nahi” it’s alright, it’s just one case. But a single case is a girl who will flinch at a temple bell, a mother who will never let go of her hand again, and a family that has to explain to an entire city why it must keep going.

In 2024, Indian courts had 206,777 rape cases for trial, but only 20,587 trials were completed, a pendency of 89.8%. Of those, 185,785 were still pending when the year ended, more than nine times the number of trials completed. The 24.4% conviction rate is measured only against trials that finished. (https://www.thestatesman.com/india/thousands-of-rape-cases-reach-indias-courts-but-how-many-end-in-conviction-what-ncrb-data-show-1503633430.html)

For girls, the picture is the same. In 2024, the conviction rate in rape cases involving girls was around 30%, with 86% of cases still pending, and in 97% of cases, the accused was known to the victim. (https://www.thedailyjagran …

author: Manila Today Staff
title: The cost of US imperialism that we are fighting against
content:
with added reports from Jessica Obciana and Kline Vergara

“Homes are destroyed, livelihoods are lost, nations are lost by interests that are made far beyond our own borders. Even now, initiatives like Pax Silica, supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors are being reordered around the needs of the US war machine, and countries like us [the Philippines] are being asked to serve as suppliers and now become their targets, rather than being allowed to decide our own development,” said Dr. Giovanni Tapang, convener of the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Network.

Various anti-imperialist groups gathered for the webinar Updates from the Resistance: The Current Situation in Iran, Palestine, Venezuela, and Cuba, co-organized by BAYAN, the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Campaign Network, to express people’s solidarity in lambasting US imperialism following its sanctions, blockades, military aggression, and other forms of intervention and coercion against the people.

“This is the war machine that we are fighting against. And as we listen to those who are on the front lines, we learn of their resistance, deepen our understanding, and together strengthen solidarity to defeat this war machine,” Tapang added.

“We have seen the case of Venezuela: how this warfare has been attacking the Global South, attacking the country, and in many, many aspects, not only the political one, military, economic, and cultural, and in social consciousness. Venezuela is under siege now,” said Richard Lobo, Venezuela’s Chargé d’Affaires.

Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at around 303 billion barrels as of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Lobo noted that US intervention in Venezuela extends beyond economic sanctions to political, military, economic, and cultural intervention.

In January 2026, the US launched Operation Absolute Resolve as a large-scale military operation in Venezuela framed around drug trafficking and national security that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores and their transfer to the United States. Such an operation also targeted Venezuelan military infrastructure across Caracas and other locations.

Months after Maduro’s capture, the US laid out an agreement to gain access and control over an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, mineral wealth, and other resources.

Meanwhile, Lobo emphasized that the situation has only amplified the resistance among Venezuelans in defending their sovereignty and their right to determine the country’s political and economic direction.

“Even though we have been under attack […] the people there in Venezuela have been resisting and have been struggling. And one thing that I can say right now is that even with the kidnapping of our president, they believe the government is still in power,” Lobo stated.

More than 5,000 civilians have been killed in the US-Israel aggression against Iran, including 168 girls who were killed when a school was struck in March this year.

“Iran is experiencing aggression by the United States and Israel since the 1979 revolution against a very corrupt government, the Shah’s government. The United States has been trying to overthrow the revolutionary government in Iran, engaging in economic warfare for 46 years,” said Dr. Foad Izadi, associate professor at the University of Tehran.

The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose government had maintained close relations with the US. The revolution fundamentally changed Iran’s relationship with the US, posing decades of diplomatic confrontation, economic sanctions, and political pressure.

“(The US) has also asked Iran to reduce its support for the Palestinian cause. As you know, Iran has been a strong supporter of Palestine. Not only with words, not only with speeches, but with military aid. Iran is the only country that is helping Palestinians with military aid,” said Dr. Izadi, noting that other governments should also learn from them by providing help to those countries fighting against aggression and genocide.

“Iran has learned that if you allow Israelis, genocidal people, the apartheid regime to get away with their crimes in Palestine, they they would want to take over the Middle East and go beyond,” he added.

title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

title: Group from Zurich takes over the Freedom for Öcalan Vigil in Strasbourg
content:
The Freedom for Öcalan Vigil, which was launched on 25 June 2012, in Strasbourg, has entered its 746thweek.


The vigil, which continues in Strasbourg, where institutions such as the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights are located, was taken over by Barış Çetin, Cihat Kalkan and Cesur Akar from Zurich.


Speaking on behalf of the demonstrators, Barış Çetin emphasized that they were protesting the conditions of isolation imposed for nearly 28 years on Abdullah Öcalan, who was imprisoned in 1999 as a result of an international conspiracy.


“We will continue until our leader’s physical freedom is secured,” Çetin said, adding, “We also want the international community to recognize the struggle taking place here and the reality of the situation. Our comrades have demonstrated their determination for 746 consecutive weeks. Our Leader’s physical freedom is of great importance to us.”


Calling on the international community to fulfill its duties and responsibilities, Çetin stated that stability and peace in the Middle East would only be possible through the freedom of Öcalan.

author: Gabby Soltura
title: University workers on strike in Brisbane
content:
National Tertiary Education Union members from Brisbane’s three major universities rallied in Queens Gardens on 8 October during a simultaneous

half-day strike

. After walking out at 11am, staff from the University of Queensland, Queensland University of Technology and Griffith University gathered in the city, chanting, “Chop from the top”! and “Union power”!

The popularity of the “chop from the top” slogan shouldn’t surprise anyone; QUT and UQ vice-chancellors

Margaret Shiel

 and

Deborah Terry

 both took home whopping $1.2 million salaries in 2025. Across the street from the rally stood a symbol of the bosses’ greed: Brisbane’s Treasury Building, which

Griffith recently bought for $67 million

, despite not having enough office space for staff. While vice-chancellors live in luxury and splurge on real estate, the workers who make our universities run are being offered crumbs.

UQ management’s most recent wage offer is

15.5 percent over 4 years

, or 3.9 percent per year, lower than current and projected inflation. Matthew Campbell, UQ branch vice-president and national councillor, told the rally that this offer would drive workers into rental stress. Management at

QUT

 and

Griffith

 have so far refused to present a pay offer.

Along with wage increases, the workers want secure jobs and sustainable working conditions.

Around 60 percent

 of workers in the industry are on casual or fixed-term contracts. “Permanent jobs for permanent work”, read one of the signs at the rally, and “Working conditions are student learning conditions” was a popular phrase among staff.

A report by the NTEU

 found that most Australian university tutorials are now two to three times larger than what academics say is optimal. It’s no wonder

engagement is declining

, as students are squeezed into overcrowded tutorials with overworked teachers who can’t cater to each student.

Workers’ declining wages reflect universities’ increasing corporatisation. Izzy, a teaching associate from UQ, told

Red Flag

:

“If you look around the world, you see the exact same thing happening in every education sector ... class sizes ballooning, workloads ballooning, forced restructuring, stripping out courses and degrees ... It’s not just one little policy here and there, it’s a systemic issue.”

Paul, a worker at UQ, spoke to

Red Flag

 about the significance of the strike involving workers from several universities: “We’ve got a hell of a long way to go ... but I really want to have a win in these struggles so that they can hopefully inspire other sections of the trade union movement to do the same thing”.

author: Ayda Issa
title: Ayda Issa: ‘People power can undo the colonialists’ maps’
content:
Ayda Issa, from the Tasmanian Palestine Advocacy Network, and a Palestinian-Australian, gave the following speech to the Lutruwita protest on October 11 to mark three years of genocide in Gaza.

Having recently returned from Lebanon, I was invited to share my reflections from the trip.

As we observe three years of accelerated genocide in Gaza, these insights feel more urgent than ever, offering a necessary testament to a deeply interconnected region.

In a gallery in Beirut, I found so-called Australia.

I went to Marfa’ Gallery to see As I Weep, an exhibition by Lamia Joreige, a Palestinian-Lebanese artist. There, in the middle of the gallery, was a replica of a mosaic from Gaza.

The Shellal Mosaic is 1500 years old. It was the floor of a church a few kilometres from Gaza City. In 1917, after the Battle of Beersheba, Australian soldiers found it while digging defensive positions near Shellal along the Wadi Ghazzeh. They glued its tiny stones onto linen canvas, lifted it from the ground and shipped it to Australia.

Since 1940, it has been set into a wall at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra. The mosaic that once decorated a holy site is now permanently displayed as a war trophy.

Joreige asks: If the mosaic were returned, who would it go back to? The villages around Shellal were destroyed in 1948 by Zionist militia and the people who lived there were expelled.

How do you return something to a land that has itself been stolen?

I had to travel to Lebanon to learn that a piece of my homeland is sitting in this country’s capital. Gaza’s mosaic is kept safe in Canberra, while Gaza itself is being turned to rubble.

Australia is not a bystander to what is happening in West Asia and it never has been.

The same Australian soldiers who took the mosaic were fighting to help Britain take Palestine. Joreige spent years reading their diaries and the work she built from them was shown at the Biennale of Sydney this year.

That victory handed Britain the power to draw lines across the region; lines that would tear families apart for the next hundred years.

In 1947, Australia helped steer the United Nations plan that carved up Palestine. Today, Australian-made parts go into the fighter jets bombing Gaza and Lebanon, while Australia continues to support Israel with impunity.

Australia will deny its complicity and responsibility, because it was built the same way: on the genocide of Aboriginal people and the theft of Aboriginal land, which this nation still refuses to fully reckon with. Terra nullius, the myth of an empty land waiting to be settled, is the very same colonial narrative used to justify the erasure and colonisation of Palestine.

This always was, and always will be, Aboriginal land. Sovereignty was never ceded.

Joreige’s exhibition is called As I Weep. For over a year, she found herself unable to cry. She watched the genocide in Gaza and the destruction of Southern Lebanon every day, speechless and powerless, yet she could not shed a tear.

Then she went to the archives in London to research the history of this violence, tracking the legacy of the Paris Peace Conference, the Zionist meetings and the Palestinian petitions that were ignored. She eventually unrolled the original Sykes–Picot map, in which Britain and France first carved up this region between them. Without warning, she cried. Her tears fell onto the paper, smudging the lines and blurring the borders that started it all.

What I kept coming back to in Lebanon was this concept of borders. Colonial lines, drawn with arrogant indifference, that divided communities and shaped what came after: both occupation and resistance.

Our friend Hanan lives in a refugee camp in Beirut. She was born in Lebanon, but her family is originally from the Hula Valley.

Before 1923, the Hula Valley and the hills of Southern Lebanon were one world. Farmers grazed their animals across neighbouring valleys. They sold their crops in the next town over. Roads ran from Tyre to Acre, from Bint Jbeil to Safad; these villages functioned as one economic unit.

Then, in 1923, Britain and France drew a line through the middle of it.

The Hula Valley went to Palestine. Nobody asked the people who lived there, who shared a life of farming, trade and community, whether this was okay. Hanan’s family ended up on the Palestinian side. That line made her northern Palestinian.

Hanan’s family was expelled, pushed north across that same line into Southern Lebanon. Their villages were …

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: NSW Socialists launch campaign with a bang!
content:
“Our message is clear: the working class isn’t going to take this shit lying down anymore”, roared Ryan Chapman, NSW Socialists candidate for the seat of Wollongong, at the launch of the party’s 2027 state election campaign.

The 300-strong crowd burst out in applause. The venue, Ashfield Town Hall, was packed to capacity.

The speakers, three of the party’s six lower-house candidates, reflected Australia’s modern, multicultural working class. The first speaker, Alma Torlakovic, candidate for the Western Sydney seat of Granville, spoke movingly of her childhood in war-torn Bosnia and Croatia. Shovan Bhattarai, candidate for the inner-west seat of Newtown, humorously described the multicultural lunchtimes at her Western Sydney primary school. Chapman spoke of growing up working class on the South Coast and joining the navy as his only option.

The housing crisis was a recurring theme. Chapman spoke about the campaign to defend the Bellambi housing estate north of Wollongong. Labor MP for the area and state planning minister Paul Scully wants to knock down the estate because it is on prized beachfront property. After detailing the eye-watering average rent rises in the inner-west, Bhattarai explained the party’s housing policy of slashing rents by 35 percent, implementing a rent freeze and building 150,000 new public housing units.

Housing is a clear example of how the NSW Labor government screws over workers to protect the profits of the rich. Labor is happy to take workers’ votes, but once in government, the party, in Torlakovic’s words, “treat Western Sydney like garbage”. The crowd was full of boos and cries of “shame” at any mention of federal or state Labor politicians.

“We are the party for the millions of people who make this city run”, declared Bhattarai. This unashamed emphasis on class politics is a refreshing antidote to a mainstream politics filled with either middle-of-the-road progressivism or vitriolic far-right bile.

After the speeches, people stuck around for food, drinks and campaign strategising. New volunteers met the campaign managers in their electorates, and people signed up for the numerous party activities planned for the coming weeks. The launch kicked off a frenetic fortnight of activity. Party activists hope this will help firmly establish the party among prospective voters and meet more people who will join the movement.

While we may not be backed by billionaires or the mainstream media, the socialist movement has always been fuelled by endless enthusiasm and dedication combined with a radical vision of a better world. If you want to be a part of that, get involved with the campaign today.

author: Madhavi Madhu
title: Malaysian PM's meeting with Myanmar coup regime leader condemned
content:
Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing visited Malaysia on October 7–8 and met with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya. Madhavi Madhu, a member of the Socialist Party of Malaysia (PSM) and a longstanding refugee rights activist, explains why this move has prompted concern and protests from human rights and refugee rights groups.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim should have maintained a stance toward Myanmar similar to his stance toward Israel, as both leaders fall into the same category: that of war criminals.

A protest was held on October 8 and a joint statement issued unequivocally rejecting and condemning the visit.

The protest was called by the Anti-Imperialist Coalition Movement (Gerakan Gabungan Anti-Imperialis, GEGAR) and the socialist student group AKSI and supported by local human rights NGOs such as Beyond Borders, Suara Rakyat Malaysia (SUARAM), Mandiri, Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH) Youth, Malaysian Islamic Youth Movement (ABIM), and the Coalition for Clean and Fair Elections (BERSIH).

They urged the Malaysian government to stand in solidarity with the people of Myanmar and refuse all formal recognition of the junta leader. They also highlighted that this presidential-level reception for the Myanmar President violates the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Five-Point Consensus.

The joint statement demanded: The immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and dialogue among all parties concerned; mediation by an ASEAN special envoy; humanitarian assistance through ASEAN mechanisms; and a visit by the ASEAN special envoy to meet with all parties concerned.

The Myanmar president stated again that the regime will only accept the deportation of "genuine citizens" of Myanmar (Rohingyans are not recognised by the regime as genuine citizens).

So while this diplomatic engagement was justified as an attempt to resolve the so-called "Rohingya issue", it has been reported that no Rohingyans have been sent back to Myanmar.

Nevertheless, the recent deportation of 1500 refugees to Myanmar and the planned deportation of another 5000 is a dangerous shortcut and a violation of the principle of non-refoulement — the international law rule that forbids returning people to a country where they face serious threats to their life or freedom.

The Malaysian Bar Association has sought the High Court's permission to challenge the government's repatriation plan.

It is important to be mindful that, apart from Rohingyan refugees seeking protection, there are other refugees from various countries in Malaysia.

A holistic, human rights-based approach is important, and a promised refugee right to work during the previous election is definitely a more dignified and humane solution for refugees and Malaysia.

The government could use readily available United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees expertise and services to manage refugees, while setting up the Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (refugee registration documentation) with more transparency.

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #300 w Emma Hagberg on ‘Comrades, Not Friends’ & The Revolutionary Front : October 8, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. Emma is the author of Comrades, Not Friends: The Revolutionary Front, Antifascism, and Class Struggle (PM Press/Working Class History, 2026), translated by Gabriel Kuhn and with a preface by Tomas Rothaus (both of whom have been previous guests of the show).

According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. Two years later, the organization folded.

See also : Presentation on the book about Revolutionära Fronten (Revolutionary Front) (April 13, 2025).

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Housing protests lead to general strike in Spain
content:
“I haven’t managed to defend my house, but I have tried so that others can learn how to defend theirs.” These were the words of an 87-year-old Madrid woman, Maricarmen, who posted a video from her hospital bed after Spanish authorities evicted her from the apartment she had lived in for the past 71 years. In the video, she promoted an upcoming protest at Madrid’s Plaza del Sol “so that we can eliminate this problem once and for all”.

Her eviction sparked a fire across the Spanish state. Within days, protesters had set up an encampment in the Plaza del Sol, famously the site of mass anti-austerity protests in 2011. They quickly spread to dozens of other cities, along with mass protests. A few days later came the first victory of the movement, when the vulture fund that had bought Maricarmen’s apartment building agreed to allow her to return with a new, eight-year contract and her rent capped at 30 percent of her pension.

But this victory only fuelled the protests. On Saturday 3 October, nationally coordinated rallies saw around half a million people protest across the country. Three days later, the country’s two major union confederations called a general strike.

Few recent examples illustrate the power of protest as clearly as the last two weeks in the Spanish state. When the authorities forced their way into Maricarmen’s apartment, she was meant to be just another of the nearly 70 people who are evicted from their homes every day across the country. But the footage of her being removed on a stretcher into an ambulance tapped into a rage that millions of people feel living at the whim of the housing market.

In Spain, it is particularly sharp. Over the last decade, rental prices have risen by more than 80 percent, according to the National Institute of Statistics. And the market is becoming increasingly concentrated in the hands of a small minority. From 2008 to 2025, the share of single property owners fell by 4 percent, while the share of people with at least ten properties rose by 35 percent, according to a recent government report.

These statistics prove the main point of the Tenants’ Union, the group leading the protests: the main problem is that under capitalism, housing is a commodity for investors to make a profit from and not a basic good provided to all people. They’ve combined this general perspective with a series of concrete demands, including automatic renewal of rental contracts, a 50 percent rent reduction, and the expropriation of empty properties.

Importantly, the union’s approach has been to spread the protests, while also raising new, more radical slogans as the movement developed. In the first few days, the movement played out under the generally defensive slogan “Not one more Maricarmen”. But as the movement exploded, the slogan shifted to “towards a general strike,” directly calling on the two major union confederations to call one.

Since Maricarmen’s eviction, the government of Pedro Sanchez’s Socialist Party (PSOE) and its junior partner Sumar, heavily influenced by the Communist Party, has scrambled to respond. It put forward two bills in parliament, including measures such as a pause on evictions until 2030 and indefinite rental contract extensions, with twelve months’ compensation for tenants if landlords break the agreement. However, the government is a minority in parliament and, among other parties, it relies on the centre-right Catalan independence party, Junts, to pass any laws. Junts joined the right to defeat the two bills.

Even though the government put forward the bills knowing they would be defeated, the fact that they included reforms like a pause on evictions until 2030 illustrates the power of the movement. Similarly, the movement’s rejection of the bills as inadequate testifies to mass popular support for genuine solutions to the housing crisis and a radical approach to achieving them. A recent poll published in elDiario.es showed 73 percent support for a general strike, 58 percent support for the main encampment in Madrid, and that 40 percent of people would be prepared to engage in a rent strike.

With the bills defeated, however, Sanchez is dissolving parliament and calling snap elections for 29 November. It’s a shrewd political move. His message will be simple: the right-wing parties used their majority to block housing reform, so a majority Socialist Party government is necessary to get real action.

But Sanchez’s record shows how fickle this message is. He is a …

author: Tamara Pearson
title: 'Never again a Mexico without us': National Indigenous Congress marks 30 years with protests
content:
"Daddy, I'm coming for you. This struggle is for you," said Jesús Plácido Domingo's daughter on Monday at the 30th anniversary meeting of the National Indigenous Congress (CNI). She looked to be perhaps six years old, and held a picture of her father, an imprisoned Indigenous activist.

Plácido was detained in July by the Mexican Army. A member of the CNI and the regional coordinator of the Indigenous and Popular Council of Guerrero-Emiliano Zapata (CIPOG-EZ), he was playing a leading role in defending Indigenous communities from organised crime and Guerrero state from environmental destruction.

Various national and international human rights organisations have criticised the arrest, and note a pattern of criminalising activists and Indigenous community leaders — particularly those that defend water rights and stand up to mining companies and other environmentally destructive corporations, and to organised crime.

On October 12, the CNI marked 534 years since the Spanish invasion of the Americas began, and 30 years since their organisation was founded. They held a three-day conference in Mexico City, with delegates from Indigenous communities around the country participating in discussions until midnight.

Allied organisations, including small farmers, human rights groups, Guatemalan migrants, environmental groups, urban and rural communities, women, community and alternative radio and media outlets, and parents of the forcibly disappeared also met and held separate discussions about how to support and strengthen Indigenous rights and resistance.

"It's important that we organise like this so that we aren't alone as Indigenous peoples and communities. The CNI is a space where we can all go to hug each other, support each other and our struggles," Tlaxco, a CNI delegate from Milpa Alta, told Green Left.

The CNI brings together peoples and tribes, including Maya, Purépecha, Mazateco, Wixárika, Yaqui, Náyeri, Nahua and at least 30 others, as well as Afro-Mexicans and Mestizo people. It practises full autonomy and strives for recognition and the rebuilding of Indigenous communities following the "permanent process of conquest that has destroyed, mutilated, fragmented, and exterminated us".

The CNI was created during forums called by the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN), in October 1996, following the San Andrés Accords between the EZLN and the Mexican government earlier that year. The agreements included ending marginalisation, recognition of Indigenous autonomy and self-determination, as well as Indigenous health, education and justice systems.

However, in 2001, following pressure by capitalists and corporate leaders, the accords were "betrayed" and wound back, says the CNI. Since then, the CNI says it practises such rights, whether the state recognises them or not.

Coming out of the conference, the CNI announced that it had adopted "important agreements to strengthen and renew the CNI, its assembly, and its work and coordination structures". It also demanded an end to the war on Palestine, that political prisoners be released, and justice for those activists that have been murdered.

The CNI stressed that original peoples, through their own assemblies and structures, are the only ones that can call and hold consultative processes, in light of the Mexican government's attempt to pass an Indigenous rights law, through "consultations" that it organises.

Thousands of CNI members and supporters also protested on October 12, shutting down three key highways around the country in rejection of the law, which they say is being "imposed" without regard for traditional authorities and general assemblies held by Indigenous communities. The proposed law comes within a history of Mexican governments imposing outside structures like mayors, municipalities and governors in order to "plunder" regions of their minerals and natural resources.

"It's important that our assemblies and the decisions we make be respected," said Tlaxco.

In Mexico, some 39 million people identify as Indigenous. They frequently experience racism, as well as institutional discrimination against their languages — especially in health and education systems. They are often at the forefront of defending their land from environmental destruction, and as a result disproportionately face human rights attacks, criminalisation, murder and forced displacement. Further, most crimes go unpunished, with systemic impunity favouring organised crime as well …

author: Lance Selfa
title: What’s up with Jacobin’s “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”?
content:
Every few months, 

Jacobin 

magazine announces what it purports to be a secret to win working-class voters based on a finding from its associated Center for Working Class Politics (CWCP). Its 14 September editorial “

Report: The Working Class Vote is Not Lost

” was the latest in this series.

CWCP’s latest innovation is the “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”, which Jacobin describes as “a data-driven road map for winning back working-class voters”. It purports to demonstrate the optimal combination of social and political appeals to move working-class voters to vote for a hypothetical Democratic candidate.

Two points should be made at the outset. When

 Jacobin

 and CWCP talk about “winning working class voters,” they don’t mean winning the working class to socialism. They mean “winning” the working class to vote for Democrats. And they define the “working class” as non-college-educated people with family incomes of between $30,000 and $150,000.

This supposedly groundbreaking survey and analysis is an exercise in political message-testing for Democratic candidates. It uses the definition of “working-class” that is the standard in lazy polling and media commentary, and thus adds no new insights. Attaching the labels of “socialist” and “working-class” doesn’t change the fact that what

 Jacobin

 and CWCP are engaged in is a completely conventional activity that regularly earns millions for Democratic Party consultants.

Without digressing into a long discussion of the inadequacies of the study’s understanding of class, it’s worth pondering why, under its definition, a non-college educated small business owner is “working class” but a college-educated nurse or K-12 teacher who is a union activist is not considered working-class. It’s the same sort of logic that 

had Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-adjacent consultants and 

Jacobin

 fawning over

 working-class avatar “oyster farmer” Graham Platner as a US Senate candidate in Maine before Platner’s campaign imploded.

The study’s key findings include “lead with working-class economics” and “adopt culture and climate positions that resonate with working-class voters”. These takeaways are supposed to increase the hypothetical Democratic candidate’s support over what it calls a “Kamala Harris-2024 style Democrat.”

For working-class economics or economic populist policies, the winning positions come from a list of ordinary policies from tuition-free community college to protecting Social Security from cuts to capping prescription-drug prices. There is nothing wrong with these proposals. But they are hardly bold. In fact, many of them are the same poll-tested offerings that Democratic Party politicians have included in their campaigns for years.

The fact that they are repackaged here as keys to victory should emphasise how little the Democrats have done to implement these when they have held power in the past. And it’s noteworthy that “Medicare for All,” the signature proposal that social democrats like 

Jacobin

 and DSA have championed for more than a decade, didn’t make the list.

But what really gives the game away are the “culture and climate” positions the analysis considers

losing

 messages for Democratic politicians. For anyone who is familiar with 

Jacobin’s

 antipathy to 

“subcultural leftism”

, the losing positions won’t surprise: reducing funding for police, “abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),” and letting “trans girls play in girls’ sports.” Other so-called “social issues,” such as defence of abortion rights, don’t significantly move the needle toward the Democrats, CWCP finds.

Mainstream Democratic Party campaigns in the midterm electoral cycle are following this script without even dialling up the “Win-o-Meter”. It’s an article of faith that serious Democratic candidates run on “kitchen-table issues” like the price of groceries and gasoline, and “don’t take the bait” by engaging with Republicans over “silly culture war” issues.
