title: Court overturns environmental approval for Birsu hydroelectric power plant in Bingöl
content:
The Administrative Court in Bingöl has overturned the environmental approval for the planned Birsu hydroelectric power plant on the Sarim River. The judges unanimously ruled that the positive environmental impact assessment (EIA) decision was unlawful. The ruling was based on an expert report that identified significant scientific and technical deficiencies in the project’s assessment.


The hydroelectric power plant, planned by the company Silvan Elektrik Üretim, is to be built on the Sarim River in the border area between the districts of Lice and Kulp in Amed (Diyarbakır) and the district of Genç in Bingöl. Villagers have been challenging the project through legal channels for several years. They fear serious consequences for the region’s water resources, biodiversity, and agricultural livelihoods.


River flow and dry periods incorrectly assessed


According to the court, the deficiencies in calculating the available water volumes are particularly serious. The river flow data used in the project are not based on measurements taken within the affected river basin. Furthermore, the average river flow was overestimated, contradicting relevant scientific findings.


Accordingly, the pronounced dry periods between June and September were not adequately taken into account in the environmental impact assessment (EIA). As a result, there is no reliable basis for determining how much water could be diverted from the river by the operation of the power plant.


According to the experts, potential impacts on the groundwater system, as well as risks associated with geological faults and blasting operations, were also not examined using appropriate calculations and models. In addition, the region’s particular topographical conditions pose further challenges. Despite the steep slopes, the environmental impact assessment does not include adequate protective measures against landslides, erosion, and avalanches.


Habitat of rare fish species under threat


The Sarim River system is of particular ecological importance. The affected area is home to the Batman loach (

Paraschistura chrysicristina

), a fish species long believed to be extinct before it was rediscovered in the region. The protected Eurasian otter also inhabits the area. According to the experts, the minimum residual water flow planned for the operation of the power plant would be insufficient to preserve aquatic habitats, particularly during the dry summer months.


Furthermore, damage to forests and ground-level vegetation could harm regional beekeeping. Honey production is an important source of livelihood for the local population. The destruction of vegetation and nectar-producing areas could significantly undermine this source of income.


The expert report also criticizes the environmental impact assessment for failing to include a comprehensive examination of the cumulative impacts on the entire river basin. As a result, the combined effects of individual interventions were not adequately assessed. The court accepted the experts’ findings and ruled that the positive environmental decision was incompatible with both legal requirements and the public interest.


Years-long legal battle over the Birsu project


The latest ruling follows several years of legal proceedings. In January 2023, the Turkish Ministry of Environment initially decided that the project did not require a comprehensive environmental impact assessment. Villagers challenged this decision in court. In March 2024, the Administrative Court in Bingöl overturned a positive environmental decision. Following further appeals by the ministry and rulings by higher courts, the case was reviewed again.


In June 2026, another on-site inspection was conducted. The expert report submitted on August 11 concluded that the project was based on insufficient scientific evidence and should not be implemented in its proposed form. It had already emerged in June that the Turkish State Hydraulic Works (DSI) had terminated the water rights agreement for Birsu after the Energy Market Regulatory Authority (EPDK) revoked the project’s preliminary license because the company had failed to fulfill its obligations.


The Environmental and Urban Law Commission of the Diyarbakır Bar Association had described this as an important victory for the years-long resistance. With the latest ruling, the project’s environmental approval has now also been overturned by the court.

author: Brian Bienkowski
title: Report Finds “Forever Chemicals” Pollute 83 Percent of 1,602 US Waterways Tested
content:
“If anything, the report dramatically understates the problem,” said a co-chair of the Great Lakes PFAS Action Network.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

If you swam, fished or paddled a lake or river in the US over the past couple of years, there’s a more than 80% chance the water contained toxic “forever chemicals,” according to a new report.

The report, published today by Environment America Research & Policy Center, found hotspots for the toxics, including the Mississippi River and Lake Ontario, and warns that this widespread pollution is likely “just the tip of the iceberg,” as it represents only a sampling of US waterways tested for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

“The report underscores what is really a much bigger problem than what most people realize,” said Tony Spaniola, co-chair of the Great Lakes PFAS Action Network. “If anything, the report dramatically understates the problem.”

The findings come as the Trump administration rolls back policies aimed at reducing PFAS in drinking water. Critics say such moves will only worsen people’s exposure to the chemicals, which are linked to some cancers, high cholesterol, decreased immune response to vaccines, liver damage, thyroid problems, reproductive issues and other health issues.

In the new report, researchers analyzed federal, state and non-profit data collected between 2022 and 2024 and found that PFAS were detected at 83% of the 1,602 US lakes, rivers and streams that were tested. There were over 114 different types of PFAS found across the waterways.

Surface water monitoring varies across the country, said John Rumpler, report co-author and the clean water director and senior attorney at the Environment America Research & Policy Center. PFAS pollution was ubiquitous in lakes and rivers that had a lot of monitoring. For example, PFAS was detected at all 39 monitoring locations on the Mississippi River in Minnesota and Wisconsin, and at all monitoring locations on and around Lake Ontario.

There were also huge PFAS spikes in some locations, with the highest levels recorded in Brunswick, Maine, near an executive airport that suffered a PFAS firefighting foam spill in 2024. State testing found a nearby surface water retention pond had PFOS — a particularly toxic type of PFAS — at 1,040,000 parts per trillion. The US Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) current maximum level allowed in drinking water is just 4 parts per trillion.

The report builds on several previous reports that have looked at PFAS in drinking water. For example, an Environmental Working Group (EWG) analysis from March found that roughly 176 million people in the US drink PFAS-polluted tap water.

However, it is important to also look at surface water alone, Rumpler said.

“For one, many communities draw their drinking water from surface waters,” he said, adding that even if state or federal policies reduced PFAS in drinking water this report shows “we are still stuck with these highly toxic chemicals in our rivers, lakes and streams.”

“And it’s there that they contaminate the fish that we eat and other wildlife,” he said.

Spaniola echoed the concerns of PFAS buildup in fish. He became involved in PFAS advocacy after learning his family’s home in Oscoda, Michigan, was in the epicenter of one of the country’s first major PFAS contamination sites due to military use of PFAS-firefighting foam for decades at the nearby Wurtsmith Air Force Base. In 2012, Oscoda put in place the first fish consumption advisory in the nation for PFAS contamination.

“The fish take in the water and PFAS, the PFAS biomagnifies within their bodies,” Spaniola said, adding that the community is “defined by water.”

“In 2016 I received notice of the contamination. I thought: if my water is not safe to drink today, it hasn’t been safe to drink for a long time,” he said. “You realize how much of a role water plays in your life every day.”

The report comes as the Trump administration has weakened or rolled back several protections meant to prevent PFAS water pollution.

The Biden administration previously set limits six types of PFAS — PFOA, PFOS, GenX, PFBS, PFNA and PFHxS — which have been linked to a variety of health harms, including cancer, heart problems and birth defects. The drinking water limits were considered landmark regulations after years of research and testing found PFAS chemicals are widespread in Americans’ drinking …

author: Ben Radford
title: The fight to save Pine Creek State Forest from NSW Forestry Corp
content:
New South Wales Forestry Corporation has begun logging in Pine Creek State Forest (PCSF), despite ongoing community efforts to protect the area as part of a critical wildlife corridor linking significant koala habitats.

Friends of Pine Creek (FoPC) is campaigning to stop logging in a 1600-hectare area of PCSF, which provides the corridor between Bongil Bongil National Park and Bindarri National Park.

FoPC facilitator Susan Harwood told Green Left the group welcomed the NSW Labor government’s Great Koala National Park (GKNP) announcement, but said the proposed boundaries leave a crucial gap between two “intergenerationally significant areas” of koala habitat.

FoPC’s “forest bridge” proposal would protect habitat connecting the two parks, allowing koalas and other species to move between the coast and tablelands, as conditions change due to fire and climate change.

Harwood said the proposed GKNP contains “a big hole in between those two national parks where extensive logging will occur”. For five years, FoPC has been asking Labor to include the entire forest bridge in the proposed national park.

Harwood said FoPC had deliberately decided on a conservative approach, only seeking to protect the areas required for ecological connectivity, rather than all of PCSF.

Despite much of the forest bridge area being classified as “plantation”, Harwood said it was planted many years ago and now provides habitat for koalas and other species. “It’s basically regenerating native forest.”

Harwood said Forestry Corp has begun clear-felling compartment 32 in the PCSF, just south of the forest bridge. However, the next area scheduled to be logged will enter the proposed koala corridor, directly alongside the proposed GKNP.

Harwood said clear-felling in this vital transport corridor will have significant impacts; log dumps and debris create major obstacles for koalas and other species to move through.

Harwood said the Save Pine Creek community group set up a blockade on Tower Road — a haulage route for the logging — on June 14 as Forestry Corp was due to start operations in PCSF.

Aunty Alison Buchanan, a Gumbaynggirr Elder, was key to the blockade. Because the blockade was located on National Parks land, rather than in state forest, National Parks and Wildlife Service officers and police ordered protesters to dismantle the camp and leave on June 23.

“They kicked Aunty Alison off her own land — it was just horrendous,” Harwood said.

In subsequent protests, people have climbed trees and locked on to machinery.

In July, an injured koala was found in compartment 32 and taken to Port Macquarie Koala Hospital, before it had to be euthanised.

Harwood sought information from Forestry Corp and the hospital about the koala, but received no response. A Freedom of Information request prompted Forestry Corp to release information last month.

The veterinary report and autopsy revealed the koala had suffered abdominal bleeding, fractured ribs, lung contusions, brain trauma and other soft tissue injuries. FoPC said the koala’s injuries were inconsistent with Forestry Corp’s account that it was “found on a pile of logs”.

Harwood said FoPC is focused on getting the forest bridge included in the GKNP. The National Park Estate (Great Koala National Park Reservations) Bill 2026 was introduced to the lower house of Parliament on October 13.

The federal Labor government, with the support of most Greens Senators, passed the controversial Improved Native Forest Management (INFM) system last month, which is claimed will help deliver the GKNP.

The carbon trading scheme sets a dangerous precedent that new national parks can only be created if money can be extracted, rather than for their ecological importance and critical role in mitigating climate change.

Premier Chris Minns, despite NSW Labor’s promises to the contrary, is now saying the GKNP is conditional on the creation of the INFM.

Harwood condemned Minns’ move as “criminal”. “To turn around and say, ‘If I don’t get money for it, then we’re not having it’, is basically what it comes down to.”

Harwood said when Labor first proposed the park, there was no mention of carbon credits. After Labor won the NSW election in 2023, environment minister Penny Sharpe rejected the use of carbon offsets, promising that the GKNP would be set up without them.

author: Bart Hawkins Kreps
title: Infrastructure, Finance, and the Sale of the Future
content:
Imagine yourself as a housing developer – an entrepreneur, a big-time player, a real deal-maker. Your people devise a plan to borrow money, buy land, design and win approval for a new subdivision, and sell 1,000 new housing units. Then, perhaps years before the houses are completed and decades before the initial mortgages are repaid, you sell your shares in the venture for a tidy profit. A neat trick, this, cashing in today on bills that others will pay long into the future.

You have become wealthier, but have you been a “wealth creator”? For that matter, are you contributing to “economic growth”? Where does the money come from for this venture: is it capital accumulated from the past, or is this money newly created the moment credit is extended by banks and off-setting debts are recorded on balance sheets?

These are among the many questions addressed by Timothy Mitchell in his new book The Alibi of Capital, out on March 10 from Verso.

Mitchell works his way through a profound rewriting of economic history and economic theory. He wants us to think carefully about who pays for what is labelled “economic growth.” Is the earning of interest some natural property of money? Why was the phrase “the economy” almost never used until the mid-20th century, while today the economy is routinely invoked as the determinant of what is politically, socially, or environmentally acceptable? Why do banks continue to invest in new fossil fuel infrastructures, in full public knowledge that these infrastructures are robbing future generations of a stable climate?

Let’s begin with a simpler question: is “financialization” an adequate term for the process by which a housing developer turns still-unbuilt houses into immediate profit? Mitchell doesn’t think so. While the creation and swapping of financial instruments is one essential part of the process, two others are equally essential. First, the process depends on the manufacture of long-lasting infrastructure. Second and equally important, there must be a legal and political framework that ensures holders of the financial instruments can enforce their claims to ongoing revenues five, ten, or even fifty years in the future.

What is often termed financialization, Mitchell, argues is really a technopolitical “apparatus of capture.”1 Mitchell writes:

“The apparatus is neither fully public nor private but combines aspects of both; is made up of both materials and ideas; deploys both law and violence; and depends upon both careful calculation and the imaginative construction of prospective worlds.” (The Alibi of Capital, page 30)

The use of an “apparatus of capture” to secure present profits from future events did not begin recently. Mitchell traces the process back hundreds of years to early joint-stock companies engaged in long-distance commerce.

Shipowners typically required credit to finance long voyages in which revenue from the sale of products would only come many months later. The letters of credit, which were also “letters of debt plus interest,” were sometimes traded, with the seller accepting a discount so that they could be paid immediately, while the buyer would receive the principal plus interest perhaps a year or more later.

The infrastructure was not very durable – ships often sank – and the time frames were short, just a few months to perhaps a couple of years. This commerce didn’t provide much scope for capturing revenue from the future. That changed in the nineteenth century with the development of railroads, which Mitchell describes as a turning point.

Railroads were large-scale durable infrastructures – and required major investment up-front. Once built they offered the promise of revenues coming in for decades. They were often built as colonial enterprises, requiring imposition of governance and military/police power to protect that revenue. The prospect of strikes also grew in importance, as workers increasingly organized against dangerous conditions, long hours, and inadequate wages; the realization of future profits required the suppression of organized labour power.

If the technical and the political factors were aligned, however, the issuance of the credit/debt associated with new railroads gave financial markets a way to buy and sell the future, earning profits immediately on services which workers would provide and customers would pay for decades later.

Railroads were followed by many other large-scale and durable infrastructures: bridges, wharves …

author: Marcos Rupérez Cerqueda
title: ‘Inner Degrowth’: An Engineer on Why the Energy Crisis and Our Inner Emptiness are the Same Problem
content:
Marcos Rupérez Cerqueda spent years as an engineer on green hydrogen projects in Spain, installing electrolysers and fuel cells, before the numbers made him stop believing in a technical fix. His new book, Inner Degrowth: From Energy Collapse to Existential Void, with a foreword by the Spanish physicist Antonio Turiel, follows that path from the energy data to a much more personal question. In this Q&A, he traces this journey and discusses his upcoming book.

I grew up inside the solution. My father is an engineer who chaired an environmental foundation, and we lived in one of the first bioclimatic houses in my region of Spain. So when I chose what to study, it felt obvious: industrial engineering, then a master’s in hydrogen in Denmark. If most of the energy that moves our civilization isn’t electricity, hydrogen looked like the perfect bridge: make it with renewables, store it, move it, use it.

Then one afternoon, in front of a spreadsheet with my business partner, I did the full count for one common chain. Around 40% of the energy is lost in the electrolyser, roughly another 10% compressing the hydrogen, and another 40 to 50% turning it back into electricity in a fuel cell. Of every 100 units of renewable electricity you put in, only 20 to 25 come out at the end. That isn’t a problem better engineering can fix. It’s thermodynamics. Hydrogen has real uses in a few narrow niches, but as a universal energy carrier, no.

Because once hydrogen fell, I started seeing the same hole everywhere. Electricity is still only around a fifth of the energy the world uses. The rest is fuel, heat and raw materials: diesel for tractors and trucks, fuel for ships and planes, heat for steel and cement, gas for fertiliser. And where you can’t electrify directly, turning electricity into something dense loses half the energy or more.

Then there is the pattern economists call the Jevons paradox: every time we make something more efficient, we end up using more of it in total. Our computers are vastly more efficient than forty years ago, and computing uses far more energy than it did then. So I stopped asking which technology saves us, and started asking why we keep needing more.

Somewhere I didn’t expect: inside my own head. In 2017 I went on a ten-day Vipassana retreat. I went in as an engineer, looking for a technique to make my mind run better. I came out not knowing who I was. What followed was the hardest year of my life. I closed my company, went back to my parents’ house and spent months coming apart.

I’m not going to romanticise it. But on the other side I saw something I couldn’t unsee: the same dynamic I had found in the energy numbers was running in my own mind. I use the image of an ideal gas. Leave it free and it fills whatever space you give it, a bottle or a whole room. The mind does the same with any capacity it gets: more time, more money, more energy. It doesn’t save them. It uses them all, and then it wants more. That is the core of the book. The energy crisis and the emptiness so many of us feel are the same phenomenon: asking material things for a fulfilment they cannot give.

It’s meant to be honest, and it includes me. Most people who follow the energy analysis to the end go through the same steps. First, technology will solve it. Then, if not technology, changing our habits. And finally, degrowth: shrinking the material economy in an organised way before collapse does it for us. That is the position most consistent with physics.

But almost none of us actually does it. Many degrowth advocates, myself included, live at the pace of the civilization we want to slow down: flights to conferences, careers that demand more output, a constant rush to tell everyone we need to slow down. It isn’t hypocrisy in a moral sense. It’s a sign that the problem isn’t mainly one of information or policy. We know where we’re heading. What fails is something more inner: the part of us that keeps reaching for the next thing.

No, and I’m wary of anything that sounds like that. In the book I’m quite hard on the personal development industry, because it often sells the opposite of what it claims: more drive, more goals, more acceleration, using the language of inner transformation. It’s the Jevons paradox applied to the soul.

Inner degrowth isn’t another technique to optimise yourself. It’s closer to letting go: less mind, less speed, less need for the next step. It won’t change the system on its own, and I don’t pretend it will …

author: Mada Masr
title: Scores killed, Sudan announces an investigation, Egypt a new phase of anti-illegal gold mining campaign
content:
In the first official comment since a mine near the Sudanese-Egyptian border was bombed on Saturday killing scores of miners, Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council

issued

 a statement on Monday to mourn the souls of “Sudanese citizens who lost their lives in the painful incident involving a number of Sudanese miners in the border area between Sudan and the Arab Republic of Egypt.”

 


Without providing further details on when, how or where the Sudanese nationals died, the executive authority that has ruled Sudan since 2019 announced that a fact-finding committee composed of members of the Sudanese Public Prosecution as well as relevant judicial and security authorities would be formed to investigate the matter. 


The council underlined that “leadership in both brotherly countries,” referring to Egypt, have “remained in continuous communication immediately after the incident occurred, ensuring the protection of lives, preserving the relationship between the two brotherly peoples, understanding the details of the incident and sharing the facts with public opinion.” 


Later on Monday evening, the Egyptian Armed Forces spokesperson released a statement announcing the implementation of the “third phase of the large-scale campaign to confront illegal gold mining in the Eastern Desert, after dropping warning leaflets on criminal elements to impose full sovereignty within the borders of the Egyptian state and protect its national resources and wealth.” 


The spokesperson similarly underlined “the depth of ties” that unite the Egyptian and Sudanese nations. 


Since the incident occurred on Saturday, Mada Masr has spoken to miners, paramedics, security officials and traders at the mining camp, which they say sits just inside the northern border of the Halayeb and Shalateen Triangle, to understand what happened. 


One of them is Abdel Bagy Nour Eddin, a shift worker at the Jabal al-Uqaydat gold mines in the Shamal al-Wadi area, north of the Halayeb Triangle.

He told Mada Masr he was at his work site when he heard warplanes flying at low altitude on Saturday morning

.


Then the mining site began to be bombed. Missiles struck the mine’s drilling sites, ore processing areas and the miners’ living quarters, triggering panic and a stampede among the miners at the site, he said.


Nour Eddin’s account was corroborated by three other eyewitnesses: Al-Taher Mohamed Ahmed, a generator technician working in the area; Al-Haj Idriss Yagoub, a trader that supplies water and food to miners from the Ansary market, in Sudan’s Ratag locality south of Halayeb; and Osman al-Gassem, a site supervisor and owner of a drilling well. 


They describe “successive waves” of strikes that made it difficult to find cover. 


The site of the strikes. Courtesy: Al-Fadel al-Rifaey’s mobile phone. Picture taken by his friend.


While many of the miners fled in panic, causing a near stampede, according to Nour Eddin, several others rushed toward the tunnels in order to rescue those injured.


Among them was Yagoub. As he approached the blast site, he saw burning machinery and people among the rubble, some dead and others in need of urgent medical help.


Ahmed, the generator operator, said a power outage in the tunnels after the explosion made movement to provide first aid to the injured and the transport of bodies to higher ground difficult.


The attack, Gassem said, came without warning, leaving workers no time to evacuate before the missiles hit.


While repeated campaigns have been carried out in recent months to push back miners in the area, which include people from Sudan, the Central African Republic and Chad, all of the sources that spoke to Mada Masr said that the scale of this attack goes far beyond anything that has happened before. 


The final toll of dead and wounded remains unclear. Miners in the area say some workers fled to the mountains after the strikes. The dispersal of workers across widely separated sites makes it harder to account for the missing and determine how many people remained within the strike zone.


However, Al-Fadel al-Rifaey, a paramedic who helped count the dead and prepare their bodies for burial at the mine, put the death toll at over 100 and added that initial estimates of the number of wounded stands at between 95 and 115 people.


Preparations for burials.

 Courtesy: Al-Fadel al-Rifaey’s mobile phone. Picture taken by his friend on October 10, between 12 pm and 1 pm

author: Unknown
title: COP31 öncesi Pasifik’ten Antalya’ya çağrı: Taku Pakasoa Deklarasyonu
content:
Birleşmiş Milletler’in Kasım’da Antalya’da gerçekleşecek 31. Taraflar Konferansı (COP31) öncesi COP toplantıları Fiji’de tamamlandı. Toplantılar, Pasifik ülkelerinin öncülüğünde 5-8 Ekim tarihleri arasında gerçekleştirildi. 


Liderler, bakanlar ve üst düzey yetkililer, 6 Ekim’de Fiji’den iklim krizinin etkilerinden en yoğun şekilde etkilenen ülkelerden biri olan Tuvalu’ya seyahat gerçekleştirdi. Deniz seviyesinin yükselmesiyle Tuvalu, iklim krizinin etkilerinden dolayı dünyanın ilk "iklim mültecilerini" gönderen ülke olarak t

arihe geçmişti. 


Fiji Başbakanı Sitiveni Rabuka, Avustralya Başbakanı Anthony Albanese ile Nepal, Tuvalu, Palau ve Mauritius dahil iklim krizi karşısında savunmasız olan birçok ülkenin liderleri ve bakanları dikkat çeken açıklamalarda bulundu.


Fiji’deki toplantılardan ayrıca “Taku Pakasoa liderler deklarasyonu” çıktı. Deklarasyona adını veren “Taku Pakasoa”, Tuvalu'da birlik olmanın ve kolektif eylemde bulunmanın gücünü ifade ediyor. 


Deklarasyon, iklim krizinin Pasifik halkları, kültürleri ve geçim kaynakları üzerindeki ağır tehdidine karşı küresel bir eylem çağrısı olarak kayıtlara geçti. 


Deklarasyon, 1,5°C sıcaklık hedefinin korunması, devlet egemenliğinin ve deniz yetki alanlarının korunması ve iklim finansmanına erişimin artırılması gerekliliğine

vurgu yapıyor.


Deklarasyonda COP28 Küresel Envanter Değerlendirmesi'nin çağrısına atıf yapıldı. Bu doğrultuda; ülkelerin kendi koşullarına göre belirleyecekleri biçimde şu küresel çabalara katkıda bulunma taahhüdü yeniden teyit edildi: 


2030’a kadar yenilenebilir enerji kapasitesini üç katına çıkarmak,


2030’a kadar enerji verimliliği iyileştirmelerinin ortalama yıllık oranını iki katına çıkarmak,


Enerji sistemlerinde fosil yakıtlardan adil, düzenli ve hakkaniyetli bir şekilde uzaklaşmak, 


Bu kritik on yılda eylemi hızlandırarak 2050’ye kadar net sıfır’a ulaşmak, 


Ayrıca okyanusun iklim düzenleyici rolünün korunması ve okyanus ısınması ile deniz seviyesi yükselmesi gibi krizlere karşı kolektif eylem talepleri de yeniden dile getirildi.


COP31 öncesinde tüm taraflar iklim krizine karşı birleşmeye davet edildi.


BM Genel Sekreteri’nin Okyanus Özel Temsilcisi Peter Thomson, okyanusların müzakerelerin arka sıralarına atılmaması gerektiğin belirterek şunları aktardı:


“Türkiye bize, gezegenin ikliminin düzenlenmesinde okyanus-iklim ilişkisinin merkezi rolünü tanıyan bir Antalya Okyanus Deklarasyonu’nun hazırlanması için çalışacağını ve bundan sonra okyanus temelli iklim eylemlerini destekleyeceğini taahhüt etmiştir.” 


Fiji, Arazi ve Maden Kaynakları Bakanı Filimoni Vosarogo ise “Bugün iklim mimarisini sıfırdan tasarlıyor olsaydınız, gezegenin en büyük fazla ısı yutağını dışarıda bırakır mıydınız? Peki ya gezegenin en büyük aktif karbon rezervuarını?” diye sordu:


“Muhtemelen hayır. Oysa yaptığımız şey buna çok yakın. Okyanus, insanlık olarak saldığımız karbondioksitin yaklaşık dörtte birini ve hapsettiğimiz fazla ısının yüzde 90’ından fazlasını emmiştir. Okyanus, gezegenin iklim düzenleyicisi ve en büyük aktif karbon yutağı; dünyanın şu anda olduğundan çok daha sıcak olmamasının tek nedeni. Ve bu hizmetin bedelini kendi sağlığıyla ödüyor.”


Genel kurulda COP31 Müzakere Başkanı ve İklim Değişikliği ve Enerji Bakanı Chris Bowen, Tuvalu ve Fiji’deki gençlerin güçlü seslerini duyduklarını belirterek deklarasyonun COP31 için çok sağlam bir çıkış noktası sunduğunu söyledi.  


"Burada söylenenler COP31'e yön verecek"


Fiji Başbakanı Sitiveni Rabuka, liderlere “Her birimiz çözümün parçası olmak zorundayız” diye seslenerek birlik mesajı verdi:


“Taku Pakasoa’nın amacı da budur. Bölgelerimizi birleştirelim, çabalarımızı birleştirelim ortak zemin

bulalım.” 


Rabuka, “Burada, Pasifik’te ve dünyanın en büyük okyanusunun sesi gibi, amacımız inovasyon adaları yaratmak, çözümleri sergilemek ve yaygınlaştırmak ve sadece sorunun ölçüldüğü bir bölge olmaktan çıkıp çözümlerin paylaşıldığı bir yer haline gelmektir” dedi. 


Fiji lideri “Liderlerin bu salonda bu akşam söyledikleri, katılım sürecini şekillendirecek ve COP31 müzakerecilerine verilecek talimatlara yön verecek” uyarısında bulundu. 


Ayrıca Rabuka, Paris Anlaşması'nda belirlenen 1,5°C kritik eşiğinin aşımını sınırlandırma konusunda net bir uyarı yaptı:


“Hukuki yükümlülüklerimize ve ahlaki hedeflerimize aykırı olan aşımı sınırlamaya kararlı olduğumuzu açık ve net biçimde göstermeliyiz.”


"1,5 derecenin elimizden kayıp gitmesine izin veremeyiz"

author: Mag
title: Rechenzentren (im KI-Boom) und die katastrophalen Umweltauswirkungen der Digitalisierung
content:
Dossier


„…

Die ETC Group leistet mit „Hinter den Wolken – Die Umweltauswirkungen der Digitalisierung“ einem neuen Bericht über die schwerwiegenden ökologischen und sozialen Risiken der Digitaltechnik, einen Beitrag zu dieser Debatte. Wir haben festgestellt, dass die Digitalisierung bestehende Ungleichheiten verschärft und eine immer stärkere Ausbeutung von Ressourcen aus der Erde, den Ozeanen und dem Weltraum erfordert. (…) Daten sind weder ätherisch noch harmlos. Sie sind ressourcenintensiv, bestehen aus Sand, Wasser, Kohle und schädlichen Chemikalien, die giftige Abfälle erzeugen. Für die Herstellung von Halbleiterchips, dem Baustein aller digitalen Dinge, werden beispielsweise Quarzsand, Quarz und hochreines Wasser benötigt. Die Fabriken für diese Chips werden auf großen Flächen gebaut, und es ist nachgewiesen, dass die Arbeiter dort schädlichen Chemikalien ausgesetzt sind

…“ span.

Meldung vom 4.9.2024 der ETC Group


 zum Bericht „Detrás de las nubes“ und mehr dazu, auch am Beispiel Lateinamerika:


Kampf um Wasser: Rechenzentren boomen – Bundesregierung will Umweltvorgaben lockern


„In Deutschland entstehen immer mehr Rechenzentren. CORRECTIV zeigt: Viele stehen ausgerechnet dort, wo Wasser im Sommer knapp wird. Ihre Abwärme verpufft meist ungenutzt. Trotzdem will die Bundesregierung die Umweltvorgaben für die Branche lockern. (…) Eine entsprechende Novelle des Energieeffizienzgesetzes wird derzeit im Bundestag beraten. Zum Beispiel soll das Zieldatum für die hundertprozentige Versorgung von Rechenzentren mit erneuerbaren Energien nach hinten verschoben werden. Außerdem sollen Betreiber Abwärme künftig nicht mehr zwingend nutzen müssen. Dabei zeigt eine CORRECTIV-Auswertung des neuen Rechenzentrenregisters des Bundeswirtschaftsministerium

, dass schon die bestehenden Anlagen Ressourcenfragen aufwerfen…“

Beitrag von Katarina Huth, Elena Kolb und Philipp Waack vom 08. Oktober 2026 bei Correctiv


 – siehe hingegen aus Österreich:


Fünf Forderungen für eine sozial-ökologische Rechenzentrumspolitik


„Rechenzentren werden mittlerweile als kritische Infrastruktur verhandelt. Doch warum, wo und wie diese gebaut werden, auf welche Energie- und Wasserressourcen sie zurückgreifen und wem sie schlussendlich nützen, ist Aushandlungssache. Dieser Beitrag stellt fünf Forderungen für eine sozial-ökologische Rechenzentrumspolitik vor, die solche Fragen demokratisch beantwortet. Ausgangspunkt ist ein kürzlich im Kurswechsel vorgestelltes Forschungs- und Handlungsprogramm für eine sozial-ökologisch planende Wirtschaftspolitik, das an Eduard März’ Arbeiten – im Anschluss an John Maynard Keynes und Karl Marx – anschließt und die Idee eines demokratischen, dritten Wegs zwischen Markt- und Planwirtschaft aufgreift. (…) 1. Rechenzentrumssektor klimaverträglich umbauen: (…) Bei Rechenzentren stammen die meisten Treibhausgasemissionen aus dem Energieverbrauch für Strom und Kühlung. Rechenzentren müssen daher als eigenständiger Sektor begriffen werden, der klimaverträglich umgebaut werden muss. Damit Rechenzentren erneuerbaren Strom beziehen können, braucht der Energiesektor einen beschleunigten Ausbau erneuerbarer Energien, der Stromnetze sowie der Speicher- und Flexibilitätsoptionen. In dem Zuge müssen die Fernwärmenetze modernisiert werden, damit sich auch die niedrigtemperierte Abwärme von Rechenzentren einspeisen lassen kann. (…) 2. Betreiber in die Pflicht nehmen: Makroökonomische Stellschrauben zielen darauf ab, den Ausbau von Rechenzentren durch gezielte staatliche Regulierung und Steuerung in gesellschaftlich orientierte Bahnen zu lenken. Dafür sollte Steuerpolitik sicherstellen, dass große Rechenzentrumsbetreiber einen angemessenen finanziellen Beitrag an ihren Standorten, insbesondere kleineren Gemeinden, leisten, in denen sie erhebliche Flächen-, Energie- und Infrastrukturressourcen beanspruchen. (…) Entgegen der Kultur der permanenten Verfügbarkeit könnten Rechenzentren dazu verpflichtet werden, ihre Stromnachfrage möglichst flexibel an Zeiten hoher Wind- und Solarstromproduktion anzupassen, denn insbesondere nicht zeitkritische Anwendungen (z. B. Backups, wissenschaftliche Forschung, KI-Training) können zeitlich verschoben werden. (…) 3. Bedarf und Kontrolle demokratisch aushandeln: (…) Rechenkapazitäten sollten an einen demokratisch verhandelten Bedarf geknüpft werden – an die Frage, welche KI und Software wir überhaupt betreiben wollen. So ist für ein spezialisiertes KI-Modell, z. B. zur Hautkrebs-Erkennung …

author: winter oak
title: Our righteous struggle
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


You’ve got to fight for what you want

For all that you believe

It’s right to fight for what we want

To live the way we please

As long as we have done our best

Then no-one can do more

And life and love and happiness

Are well worth fighting for


These lyrics, together with the stirring tune to which they are set, made a great impression on me when I was a boy.


The song

Fight

 by The Musketeers, released as a single in 1969, was the

theme music

 for

The Flashing Blade

, the English version of a French TV series called

Le Chevalier Tempête

. [1]


The story is based on historical events during the 17th century War of the Mantuan Succession between France and Spain, but I do not think the details of the plot interested me much – it was the song that I loved!


I knew somehow – in my bones, in my blood, in my guts – that what the words were saying was both true and important.


The song’s message was still ringing in my ears when I first launched myself, as a teenager, into my ongoing – but so far unsuccessful – efforts to bring down the venal and usurious globalist system.


I must have already come across the same spirit in the tales of Robin Hood, William Tell and other heroes and so I suppose one could argue that the outlook had been implanted in me by the cultural environment in which I grew up.


But I would say, rather, that it was already there at my birth – in the innate pattern of my mind, heart and soul – and that external stimuli like the song merely activated a thought that was waiting to be thought, provided the means by which an unconscious attitude became conscious.


And, even though not everyone thinks that way, I would say that we are looking here at an idea – a principle, rather – that generally forms part of our collective culture, in Europe and elsewhere.


We see it, for instance, in medieval Norse culture, in the

Elder Edda

 of Saemund Sigfusson:


“A cowardly man thinks he will ever live, if warfare he avoids; but old age will give him no peace, though spears may spare him”.

 [2]


It is also present, of course, in the Arthurian legends, as I noticed when re-reading a book that I have kept hold of since my childhood –

King Arthur and His Knights of the Round Table

 by Roger Lancelyn Green (1918-1987), a friend and

biographer

 of the author C.S. Lewis. [3]


Although this was published by Penguin under the “Puffin” label aimed at younger readers, it is a serious and eloquent re-telling based on Sir Thomas Malory’s famous account and weaving in material from various other sources.


I was amused to see the title of the aforementioned TV series make an appearance when Merlin the magician/druid announces, regarding young Arthur: “In Avalon the elves are forging Excalibur to be the sword of his right – the clean flashing blade that shall be raised only in the cause of right, shining on the earth until the time comes when they shall call it back again”. [4]


Likewise, Sir Launcelot of the Lake tells Sir Percivale of Wales: “Not in great deeds of arms lies the true worth of knighthood – rather in the heart of the doer of such deeds: if he be pure and humble, doing all things to the glory of God and to bring that glory and that peace throughout our holy kingdom of Logres”. [5]


At the inauguration of the Round Table, Merlin declares: “All of you, and those who shall sit afterwards at this Table, are the Knights of Logres, and for the glory of Logres, the Realm of Righteousness, do not ever depart from the high virtues of this realm.


“Do no outrage nor murder nor any cruel or wicked thing; fly from treason and all untruthfulness and dishonest dealing; give mercy unto those who seek it – or sit no more at this Table.


“And always give all the help in your power to ladies and damsels, go out to succour gentlewomen and widows, turn from all else to right any wrong done to any woman in the world – and never, on pain of death and eternal disgrace, do you any ill thing to a woman, or suffer it to be done. Nor, for love or gain, fight in any quarrel that is not just and righteous”. [6]


By the way, the sign of Logres – “the land of true good and piety, nobleness and right living” [7] – is described by Lancelyn Green as being a five-pointed star [8] like the one that forms the organic radical logo below, together, in our case, with the rising sun of renewal and the greenery of life.

author: Kay Pacha / Equipo Pueblos Originarios del SERPAJ
title: Lecko Zamora: una voz Wichí por el 12 de octubre
content:
Y llegamos una vez más al 12 de octubre, fecha muy simbólica y oportuna para hacer recordar que significó y significa para los pueblos originarios, que fue el comienzo de una invasión, un genocidio y un sistema colonizante en todo sentido.


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/12-de-octubre.mp3


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/12-de-octubre.mp3


Descargar archivo


Pero ahora, a pesar que se quiera volver al Día de la Raza, los hermanos y hermanas aprovechan la oportunidad para hace oír sus voces, sus reclamos y en general denunciar la situación de racismo, violencia y despojo territorial que vienen sufriendo.


Por eso en esta oportunidad han tenido lugar a lo largo y ancho de nuestro país, numerosos actos, movilizaciones  y marchas en donde se manifestaron las denuncias y reclamos por estas situaciones.


Uno de los reclamos urgentes en estos momentos es el cese de los desalojos de comunidades de diversos pueblos y territorios. Todos los documentos que se conocieron por estos días difunden ampliamente la difícil situación que están atravesando varias comunidades, como ser la Lof Melo en la Provincia de Neuquén.


Afortunadamente la existencia de estas movilizaciones revela el espíritu de resistencia y lucha de las comunidades, que utilizan todas las herramientas necesarias en su defensa y contra un aparato jurídico y represivo que  responde a los intereses de quienes ambicionan sus territorios para sus ambiciones de lucro y de explotación de sus bienes naturales.


Todas estas situaciones denunciadas son bien conocidas y siempre las difundimos, pero en esta oportunidad queremos compartirle algo diferente, algo que si bien es una denuncia en general, está hecha con una hermosa y poética presentación.


Presentamos la voz de Lecko Zamora, escritor, artista, gestor cultural y referente de la cultura wichí, quien expresa en forma muy personal lo que todos venimos denunciando sobre el 12 de octubre.


El Micro Kay Pacha se realiza con el apoyo de la organización Otto per Mille-Chiessa Valdense.


La entrada

Lecko Zamora: una voz Wichí por el 12 de octubre

 se publicó primero en

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

author: Michael Beltran
title: America’s AI ambitions threaten Indigenous lands in the Philippines
content:
This is an original story by

Mongabay

 republished through the Indigenous News Alliance.


Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. arrived at the Grand Hyatt Manila on Sept. 10 to address hundreds of foreign business representatives assembled for the Luzon Economic Corridor investors’ forum.


Outside the hotel, hundreds of demonstrators had also gathered, carrying signs that read “No to Pax Silica!” The scene reflected both the government’s ambitious plans to ride the artificial intelligence wave and deep ambivalence in civil society.


Police confronted the crowd, shoving them with riot shields and batons on the street outside the hotel lobby. Activists say police injured at least 27 protesters and arrested five. Police, meanwhile, reported minor cuts and injuries to 16 personnel. 


Protester Jona Yang, from the activist-scientist group AGHAM, said she was negotiating with the police to cool tensions when they arrested her. “We want the Marcos government and investors to see the outrage all of this has caused,” Yang told Mongabay. “They’re taking away our resources and our lands.”


The Luzon Economic Corridor, or LEC, is an economic initiative focused on the Philippines’ biggest island, begun in 2024. Pax Silica, the U.S.-led global pact to build an AI and semiconductor supply chain that is not reliant on China, includes the LEC. In April, Washington and Manila announced plans to

build a 4,000-acre high-tech manufacturing hub

 in the Central Luzon region.


Pax Silica has become a lightning rod for political and environmental contentions. The government maintains it’s a boon for the Philippine economy. But opponents of the project, including Indigenous and local communities living on the land designated for the project, say it’s an international land and resource grab in the name of U.S. AI ambitions.


U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Manila in July to affirm bilateral commitment to the project, with a final agreement slated for signing in November.


At the LEC forum, Pax Silica was discussed behind closed doors, and officials gave few details about its future. Angela Ignacio, an undersecretary at the Philippine Department of Finance, told reporters it would be premature to share any details on Pax Silica before plans are finalized. But she did call it a chance for the Philippines to become a “global player when it comes to technologies that will shape the future.”


Heather Variava, senior adviser to the U.S. State Department’s Bureau of Economic, Energy, and Business Affairs, added that “the goal of the U.S. is always to be an additive, to bring more power, to bring water, to bring more benefits to the Philippines.”


The Pax Silica hub will be built within

New Clark City

, a government-planned “smart” city inside the greater 79,000-acre Clark area, a former U.S. military complex. Clark is titled and managed by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority, or BCDA, an office under the supervision of the president. At a press briefing, development authority chief Joshua Bingcang shared a “conservative” estimate that the facility would need around 3 gigawatts of energy to run. He also said that it would be green and mainly solar powered.


“We are blessed with 300 days of sunshine,” Bingcang added.


Running consistently, the Pax Silica facility would demand about 26.3 terawatt-hours each year; by contrast, the Philippines’ entire service sector consumed about

28 TWh

 in 2024.


Giovanni Tapang, former dean at the University of the Philippines’ College of Science and a convenor of the Network Opposed (NO) to Pax Silica, told Mongabay that the Philippines has the “most to lose” among the 25 nations involved in the pact as it chains domestic resources to U.S. policies. “How many thousands of hectares will they be taking from farmers to build solar panels? And if we’re generating all this clean energy, why let the U.S. use it instead of local households?” Tapang said.


The development authority initially said that data centers could be part of the Pax Silica. But Bingcang and the

president’s office later denied this

 in a September press briefing where he emphasized it would be a semiconductor facility.


A document shared at the LEC forum listed data centers as part of the planned infrastructure in New Clark City. It did not specify whether the data centers would be built inside the Pax Silica hub.


Bingcang said the Pax Silica hub would also consume about 16 million to 24 million …

author: Johnnie Jae
title: Indigenous People Are Resisting Erasure From Schools, Media, and Our Land
content:
Joining the fight against our erasure helps Native communities defend our right to be seen, heard, and counted.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas that the Indigenous Lucayan people called Guanahani. He continued on to Cuba and Hispaniola and, on later voyages, to other parts of the Caribbean, but he never set foot in what is now the continental United States. It makes little sense for a country to honor a man who never reached it, and even less to credit him with discovering a place that millions of people already called home. And it makes even less given what Columbus actually did in the places where he stepped foot: He rounded up Indigenous people in the Caribbean, chained them, and sent them as slaves to Spain. And when Indigenous communities rose up in resistance, he ordered his soldiers to “spread terror,” maiming and slaughtering civilians en masse using firearms, dogs, swords, and pikes.

But despite all this, in 1937, the United States established a federal holiday in his name anyway.

Native people have been fighting the sanitization of Columbus’s story for decades. The idea of replacing Columbus Day arose as early as 1977, when Indigenous representatives raised it at a United Nations conference in Geneva.

In 1990, South Dakota renamed the day Native Americans’ Day. The change began with Oglala Lakota newspaper publisher Tim Giago, whose columns challenged Governor George Mickelson to mark the centennial of the Wounded Knee massacre with a “Year of Reconciliation” and to give the October holiday to Native people, proposals Mickelson took to tribal leaders and then to the legislature.

Two years later, as the country marked 500 years since Columbus landed, the city of Berkeley, California, adopted Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Bay Area Native organizers and their allies, returning from a 1990 gathering of Indigenous nations in Quito, Ecuador, formed a coalition called Resistance 500 and won official taskforce status from the City Council, which then unanimously adopted their recommendation to replace Columbus Day. Today at least 17 states and more than 100 cities recognize it, and in 2021, Joe Biden became the first president to formally proclaim it.

Then, the next White House reversed course. In October 2025, President Trump moved to “reclaim” Columbus’s legacy from those he termed “left-wing arsonists,” though he never mentioned Indigenous Peoples’ Day by name.

Native people have been fighting the sanitization of Columbus’s story for decades.

Columbus Day tells a story that skips what came before 1492 and what came after. Before the United States existed, Indigenous nations governed and cared for these lands. Colonization brought land theft, forced removal, and government policies designed to break those nations and sever Native people from their languages, cultures, communities, and homelands.

The people carrying out those policies often stated their intentions openly. In 1851, California’s first governor, Peter Burnett, told state legislators that a war of extermination would continue “until the Indian race becomes extinct.” In 1892, Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, described the purpose of federal boarding schools in one line: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.”

Indigenous Peoples’ Day marks that failure. It also arrives during a new wave of attempted erasure across Indian Country. The methods are different, but the questions are familiar. Who gets counted? Who gets to tell our history? Who gets to speak for Native people? Who decides what happens to Indigenous land, water, and culture?

When this country attempts to count Native people, it always seems to fall short. Pollsters ostensibly skip us because oursample size is too small to report. On election night in 2020, a national network put Native voters on screen as “something else.”

The U.S. census, for all its flaws, at least asks. It lets us check a box and write in the name of our tribe.

Now the federal government wants to stop asking altogether. On September 10, 2026, the Census Bureau proposed dropping the race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 census. Race has been on the form since the first count in 1790, though for much of that time we were left out. Until 1940, the government excluded “Indians …

author: Mat Costanzo
title: What We Seek in Therapy May be Lost to Time
content:
F

inishing my work day, I head home. I think about quickly changing clothes and going to the gym. I care about my health and value fitness. Yet, work was long and in the back of my head I know: I can always go tomorrow. As I turn the corner onto Skidaway Rd, I pass a large gas station. Unbidden, my mind rapidly recalls the food waiting in my kitchen. Nothing I’m particularly excited about. I don’t have ingredients, really. Only ready options like cereal, chicken cutlets, some packaged Risotto. I don’t really know what I’d do with groceries because beyond sauteed chicken and spinach or milk and cereal, I don’t actually know how to cook. I make a quick turn into the parking lot, jump out and am back in my car heading home with some hot chicken tenders. How convenient and delicious, I think.


It’s just myself and my dog at home these days. His needs are the only ones outside my own that place demands on me. So, after finishing my chicken, which I share with Petey, I put on some comfortable clothes and drive him to the dog park. I reflect on the strangeness of this obligation. There are so few left that haven’t been outsourced. I’m glad to be going, though. The dog park is one place I see people regularly. I look forward to seeing them. I used to work in person at hospitals and saw people there, but Covid changed that. I’ve worked remote ever since. Sometimes I consider it a blessing, but more and more, I miss those people, the opportunity to put on the clothes I like, the obligation to navigate numerous relationships. It seems I don’t need those clothes very often anymore, nor the skill I learned in social situations, scripted though they may have been.


But the dog park forces me to interact. While I’m there, chatting with these people whom I’d otherwise never have met, we get on the subject of the future. Waymo is brought up. Self-driving cars. I say, “Once they see the data on accidents by self-driving cars beside accidents by human drivers, I’m sure they’ll feel obligated to insist we all use self-driving cars. The safety data will be undeniable.”


So, we sit quietly with that for a moment, thinking the same thought: we

like

 driving, and we’ll likely lose it. Of course, the argument in favor of letting AI drive is clear: fewer accidents, fewer injuries, fewer deaths. But we all see what we’ll lose as well. Controlling the car, a feeling of freedom and vitality from maneuvering effectively. Someone says, “They probably said the same thing about horses when cars came along.” A quick question to ChatGPT brings back a volume of quotes from the early 20th century. One said, “The pleasure of driving depends on the lively communication, the give and take between man and horse. It is a kind of conversation carried on by means of the reins and bit” (

The Horse: His Breeding, Care and Treatment,

 1917). I read it aloud and we fall silent again. I look at the dogs, thinking

How long till I don’t need to come here?


Image created by AI tool


The point is that progress removes the conditions that made skills, relationships, meaning, and purpose necessary. With many solutions, a valued part of life ceases to be required. The problems that were solved deserved solving; the cost of solving them went uncounted. When a condition that repeatedly demanded a capacity disappears, the capacity may never develop, may weaken, or may survive only in displaced form.


As far back as the advent of writing, some cultures were wary of what might be lost when knowledge was moved outside the people who carried it. Caesar wrote that the Druids deliberately refused to commit their teachings to writing, despite using writing for other purposes, partly because they believed reliance on it would weaken learning and memory. Plato raised a similar concern in the

Phaedrus

: that storing knowledge in external marks could leave people with the appearance of knowing. It’s easy to imagine their concerns around diluting the richness of their shared symbolic world.


We’ve all noticed the vitriol in our online social media interactions. When I think of the jibes and blunt angry language, I can’t help but think of the social dexterity I first noticed in films from the 1930s and 40s. The movies made it visible to me, but the capacity wasn’t invented by screenwriters. Contemporary etiquette books devoted entire chapters to learning how to talk, disagree and move comfortably through complicated social situations. Whatever we think of those rules now …

author: Unknown
title: Sağlık Bakanlığı: Eşitsizlikleri devam ettirmekte kararlıyız!
content:
Sağlık Bakanlığı İstatistik Yıllığı (SBİY) 2025 Haber Bülteni, 30 Eylül 2025, çarşamba günü, saat 17:00’de 

(!)

 yayımlandı. İlki 12 yıl önce, 2014 yılında yine eylül ayının son günü SBİY 2013 Haber Bülteni olarak yayımlanmıştı. Bülten, istatistik yıllığından yaklaşık üç, dört ay önce daha az sayıdaki veri grubunu kapsayacak şekilde yayımlanıyor. Bununla birlikte, ölümlülük, aşılama ve hizmet kullanımıyla ilgili bir önceki yılın verilerine 9-10 ay sonra da olsa ulaşabilmiş oluyoruz. Ve Türkiye’nin dokuz ilinin bulunduğu coğrafyada yaşayanların, AKP’li yılların bundan önceki 16 yılında olduğu gibi, 17nci yılında da değişmeyen bir biçimde sağlık ve sosyoekonomik eşitsizlere mahkûm edilmiş olduğunu görüyoruz. Bu haftaki yazıda söz konusu durumu ve AKP’li Sağlık Bakanlığı’nın verileri kendine saklamak gibi bir özelliğini kendilerinin sunduğu kaynaklar üzerinden ele alacağım.


ERİŞ BİLALOĞLU YAZDI


Yeni Bir Sıfırlama Çabası mı: Türkiye’de Bebek Ölüm Hızı


29 Ocak 2015


AKP’li bakanlık verileri kendine saklıyor


AKP tarafından 2002 yılında kurulan 58. Hükümet’e kadar sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili veriler yıllardır istatistik yıllıklarıyla düzenli olarak kamuoyuyla paylaşılıyordu. Ancak

58. Hükümet ve o kabinenin Sağlık Bakanı Recep Akdağ ile birlikte, sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili veriler kamuoyundan 2011 yılına kadar saklandı,

paylaşılmadı. Dünya Sağlık Örgütü başta olmak üzere, Türkiye’nin üyesi olduğu uluslararası kuruluşların talebi üzerine, bir AKP Hükümeti ve Sağlık Bakanı olarak ilk defa 2011 yılında, 2008 yılına ait veriler “Sağlık Bakanlığı Sağlık İstatistikleri Yıllığı 2008” başlığında Bakan Akdağ’ın önsözüyle yayımlandı. O nedenle Türkiye’nin 2003-2007 yıllarına ait sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili verileri diğer yıllar gibi düzenli bir biçimde bugüne kadar paylaşılmadı.


Sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili istatistikler, 2011 yılından sonra, Sağlık Bakanlığı ve Türkiye İstatistik Kurumu (TÜİK) tarafından düzenli olarak yayımlanıyor. TÜİK, özelikle doğurganlık ve ölümlülükle ilgili verileri Merkezi Nüfus İdaresi Sistemi (MERNİS) üzerinden iller düzeyinde, sağlık harcamalarıyla ilgili verileri Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı ile Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu (SGK) ve yerel yönetimlerden ve “Hanehalkı Bütçe Anketi” çalışması üzerinden, hastalıklarla ilgili verileri de “Türkiye Sağlık Araştırması” üzerinden sağlıyor. Sağlık Bakanlığı da bu verileri kullanıp yaptığı hesaplamaları ve sağlık kurumları, sağlık emekçileri, ilaç, sağlık hizmetleri kullanımı vb. verileri Türkiye’nin makro düzeyde ekonomik ve sosyo-ekonomik yapıya göre gruplandığı 12 bölge, İstatistiki Bölge Bilgileri Sınıflaması-1 (İBBS-1), üzerinden paylaşıyor. Bununla birlikte, 

Sağlık Bakanlığı kaynakları üzerinden 81 ilden herhangi birinin sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleri verilerini, durumunu öğrenebilmek mümkün olamıyor.

Çünkü Sağlık Bakanlığı illerin verilerini yayımlamayı uzun zamandır tercih etmiyor.


Tabip Odası Bebek Ölümlerine Önlem Paketini Açıkladı


25 Eylül 2008


Bebek ölüm hızı önemli bir toplumsal sağlık düzeyi göstergesidir


Toplumların sağlık düzeyinin değerlendirilmesi ve izlenebilmesi amacıyla “bebek ölüm hızı”, “beş yaş altı ölüm hızı” ve “doğumda beklenen yaşam süresi” uluslararası alanda sıklıkla kullanılan, kabul görmüş üç değişkendir. Bunlar aynı zamanda, ülkelerin gelişmişlik düzeyi göstergeleri arasında da yer almaktadır. Çünkü, bu üç gösterge bir ülkede, bölgede, ilde vb. öncelikle beslenme, barınma, alt yapı ve eğitim başta olmak üzere, sosyoekonomik koşulların durumu ve sağlık hizmetlerinin ulaşılabilir olup olmamasıyla sağlık hizmetlerinin niteliğinden doğrudan etkilenmektedir.


Gebeliğin herhangi bir döneminde, canlı doğan bebeğin, birinci doğum gününü göremeden ölmesi, nüfus bilim (demografi) ve tıp alanında bebek ölümü olarak kabul edilmekte, tanımlanmaktadır. Bir ilde, bölgede ve/veya ülkede yıl içinde canlı doğan her bin bebekten kaçının birinci doğum gününü göremeden öldüğü de bebek ölüm hızı olarak tanımlanmaktadır. ilk ay içinde gerçekleşen

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars — But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
A lawsuit in Illinois charges that prisons blocking videophone capabilities violate the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in New York, California, and Illinois — have distributed tens of thousands of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often charged predatory fees for accessing these benefits). As of 2022, 25 state prison systems had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center.

But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind.

Disability justice organization HEARD points out that it’s unknown how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a 2015 report by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in state and federal prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.

Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC) distributed tablets to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).

In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.

“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a press release announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”

There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the complaint filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist.

“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told Truthout. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.”

IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC announced it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release, IDOC said that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.”

But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs.

Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint.

“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”

The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.

“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”

These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.

author: Unknown
title: Antiterro et psychiatrie : un bref récap de la loi Rodwell
content:
Quelques infos sur la loi Rodwell, ou loi Philippine, passée fin juillet 2026


La loi Rodwell ou loi Philippine (oui oui, Philippine comme la meuf assassinée par un type sortant de

CRA

 en septembre 2024, provoquant une campagne de haine raciste et xénophobe), ou loi du 27 juillet 2026, est une loi qui mixe le droit pénal, le droit de la santé et le droit des étrangers pour «

 

prévenir le passage à l'acte terroriste

 

» - ambiance minority report.


Pour résumer, c'est un renforcement ou une adaptation de mesures répressives qui étaient déjà souvent présentes - et mises en place - dans le droit français : il y a peu de choses complètement nouvelles. On trouve intéressant d'analyser ici quelques unes de ses principales mesures, notamment du fait des liens étroits entre répression et psychiatrie, qui sont très explicites dans la loi.


La loi met en place :


1) Une rétention de sûreté terroriste à l'issue de la peine : enfermement d'une personne dans des établissements «

 

socio-médico-judiciaires de sûreté

 

» après l'exécution complète de sa peine. Cette mesure concernerait les personnes condamnées à une peine d'au moins quinze ans pour un crime de terrorisme. Une commission, peu avant la fin de la peine, doit déterminer si la personne présente une «

 

particulière dangerosité

 

», concept carrément flou évalué notamment sur des critères encore plus flous comme le «

 

risque de récidive

 

», «

 

l'adhésion persistante à une idéologie terroriste

 

» et un «

 

trouble grave de la personnalité

 

»...


Comme pour la plupart des mesures d'enfermement dans des établissements assimilables à des

HP

, il n'y a pas de durée maximale prévue par la loi - en général c'est un an, reconductible à peu près indéfiniment (le principe c'est que la personne y reste jusqu'à ce qu'elle ne représente plus un danger pour la société...)


Il est intéressant de noter que des mesures similaires existaient déjà depuis 2008 pour certains crimes de «

 

droit commun

 

» : meurtre, viol, torture, actes de barbarie, séquestration et enlèvement. Ça concernerait très peu de personnes actuellement, mais on se doute que cette loi va permettre de renflouer les dispositifs existants.


2) Une injonction préfectorale d'examen psychiatrique : de ce qu'on comprend, à n'importe quel moment (pas besoin d'être en gav ou en examen, ou même d'avoir «

 

troublé l'ordre public

 

»), le préfet peut obliger une personne à subir un examen psychiatrique approfondi - par un psychiatre figurant sur une liste établie par la cour d'appel. C'est vraiment sur la base de suspicion de «

 

radicalisation

 

» et de «

 

troubles mentaux

 

». Et bon quand on sait que les fichiers d'Hopsyweb sur les personnes hospitalisées sous contraintes sont croisés avec ceux des «

 

fichiers de traitement des signalements pour la prévention de la radicalisation à caractère terroriste

 

», cela fait déjà une bonne liste de potentiels suspects. Si le certificat médical émis par le psychiatre va dans ce sens, le préfet peut décider d'interner la personne en

HP

 sans son consentement (mais ça, ça existait déjà bien avant). Autant préciser que cette visite au toubib n'est pas facultative : on a la possibilité de faire appel au juge administratif en théorie, mais si on refuse de voir le psychiatre ou si on ne s'y présente pas dans le délai imparti, c'est perquiz, pour se rendre au rendez-vous sous escorte.


3) Une mesure judiciaire de rétention pour les condamnés de droit commun «

 

radicalisés

 

» - là, la loi viserait spécifiquement les gens qui seraient passés par la taule (au moins 10 ans) pour des faits non-liés au terrorisme, mais se seraient «

 

radicalisés

 

» en prison. Là encore, en fin de peine, une commission évalue si le détenu présente une «

 

dangerosité particulière

 

». Si oui, et contrairement à la rétention de sûreté terroriste, la personne n'est pas ré-enfermée, mais elle a droit à l'équivalent d'un suivi

SPIP

 très renforcé, pour veiller à sa «

 

réintégration

 

» : ce suivi peut inclure une obligation de taff ou de formation, un suivi psychiatrique, l'obligation d'habiter dans une zone déterminée... En gros, un contrôle très approfondi de la vie de la personne dans ses moindres aspects.


4) Le renforcement des

MICAS

 (avec notamment moins de possibilités de les contester). Ce sont les «

 

Mesures Individuelles de Contrôle Administratif et de Surveillance

 

», qui incluent déjà la possibilité de …

title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.


The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.


About the session


Date & time:


15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 Trans communities and activists 


Register here


What the session will cover 


Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.


The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? What community networks and resources are already available? What might help or hinder efforts to build similar community-led care?

content:
Alors que la jeunesse française embrase le pays, nous avons interviewé Christian Ingrao pour son nouveau livre

Le Temps des promesses

. La situation présente est le produit d'une lente glaciation de l'espérance qui avait été annoncée non par des prophètes, mais par des historiens, des économistes, des ingénieurs agronomes, et toutes ces littératures grises qui enregistrent, en même temps qu'elles font, l'espérance et ses vacillements. Nous vivons les derniers moments d'une série de promesses nées aux lendemains de la mutation anthropologique des guerres mondiales, et dont la force d'élan et d'entraînement s'est tarie au tournant des années 1980. En réactivant une méthode matérialiste inspirée de Engels et Marx, Ingrao parvient à reconstruire la « sociogenèse de l'espérance », depuis une multitude d'observatoires, dont le temps présent nous dit la fin.

author: Yaakov Ophir, PhD
title: Let There Be Light: Before Psychiatry Writes Its Next DSM
content:
F

or all the years I have spent studying the DSM, the diagnostic manual so often called “the bible of psychiatry,” I never really stopped to think about that nickname. I assumed it referred to authority: the canonical text that tells clinicians what counts as a mental disorder and how it should be diagnosed.


But while writing

my recent Feature for the

British Journal of Psychiatry

1

 (a prominent journal within mainstream academic psychiatry), the metaphor suddenly struck me differently. Perhaps the DSM resembles a bible for another reason too. Its words have something of a “Let there be light” quality.


This is hardly a discovery of mine. Many of psychiatry’s most important critics were thinking along these lines long before I was. But working closely with the

changing language of successive DSM editions

2

 made the idea strikingly concrete for me.


Psychiatric diagnoses, as

Mad in America

 readers know all too well, are unusual things. They are largely classificatory constructs built around patterns of experience and behavior. We do not diagnose them through blood tests, brain scans, or other biomarkers that can independently confirm the diagnosis.


And that is what makes the wording so unusually powerful. Change a small thing in the definition, and watch what happens. Who meets the diagnosis changes. Which treatments are offered changes. What researchers study changes. How schools and families respond changes. Sometimes even how people understand themselves changes. Of course, suffering, difficulties, and human traits are not created by the DSM. But a psychiatric label can create a new clinical reality around them.


The DSM, therefore, resembles the Bible in its power to shape reality. But unlike the Bible, its words are rewritten again and again. One particularly consequential rewriting came in 1980, with the publication of the third edition of the DSM.

3

 DSM-III is widely remembered as a turning point in modern psychiatry.

4

 It was meant to address serious problems in the existing classificatory system and make psychiatric diagnosis more consistent and more reliable. It was, in many ways, psychiatry’s scientific revolution. The DSM had undergone a major facelift. Psychiatry’s “bible” now carried the aura of science. If a diagnosis appeared in its pages, it could feel all the more real. Science, after all, had put it there.


Image created with AI tool


Let There Be ADHD


One of the diagnoses born in this new “scientific” edition was Attention Deficit Disorder, the diagnostic construct that would later become ADHD. DSM-III brought several earlier childhood labels (e.g., Hyperkinetic Reaction of Childhood, Minimal Brain Dysfunction) together under a single diagnostic construct, on the grounds that attentional difficulties were prominent across them. Of course, children had struggled with attention, activity, and behavior long before 1980. But now those difficulties had a new name. And once that name entered the DSM, it began to take on a clinical life of its own (for a broader discussion, see our review of the philosophical foundations of narrative therapy for ADHD).

5


Of course, that fact alone does not mean that the original formulation was unjustified. But ADHD would go on to become an unusually revealing case study of psychiatric classification itself. Our systematic analysis of every ADHD-related passage across successive DSM editions

2

 revealed a pattern of changes that touched almost every major fault line in psychiatric classification, from the boundary between normality and pathology to the tension between nature and nurture. Across just four decades, six major shifts stand out:


ADHD has shifted from a primarily behavioral disorder to a neurodevelopmental condition emphasizing biological and cognitive underpinnings.


Initially conceptualized as a disorder of young boys, ADHD has evolved into a lifespan condition spanning ages and genders. Reported prevalence in children increased from 3% to 7.2%, while the male-to-female ratio declined from 10:1 to 2:1. DSM-5 recognized adult ADHD (2.5% prevalence), lowered symptom thresholds for older individuals, and extended the age-of-onset criterion from 7 to 12 years.


The definition of impairment has broadened beyond academic difficulties to include occupational, social, and emotional domains. Later editions also lowered the threshold for impairment, allowing diagnosis even in cases of relatively minor functional difficulties …
